HEALTH AND SAFETY (PIKE RIVER IMPLEMENTATION) BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I move, That the Health and Safety
(Pike River Implementation) Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee to consider the bill, and at the appropriate time I intend
to move that the bill be reported to the House by 30 October 2013.
This bill is part of the Government’s commitment to implement the
recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy by
the end of 2013. The bill paves the way for a new set of mining regulations that will
improve health and safety in the mining industry and bring New Zealand’s regulation of
11374 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
mining health and safety in line with intern ational best practice. We owe this to the
workers who lost their lives at Pike River, and to their families, and to all current and
future workers in the mining industry.
The bill before us today is an omnibus b ill. It addresses those recommendations of
the royal commission that require new or amende d primary legislation. It will establish
a new stand-alone Crown agent, WorkSafe New Zealand, to focus on workplace health
and safety, it will amend the Health and Safe ty in Employment Act, and it will replace
the Mines Rescue Trust Act.
The first part of this bill, as I have said, establishes WorkSafe New Zealand. The
creation of a stand-alone Crown agent with a dedicated focus on health and safety was a
key recommendation of both the royal comm ission and the Independent Taskforce on
Workplace Health and Safety. It signals the st ep change required in the regulation of
health and safety in the workplace.
WorkSafe New Zealand will play a significant role in achieving this Government’s
target of reducing workplace fatalities a nd serious injury rates by 25 percent by 2020.
This goal should be representative of the type of approach that this new regulator should
take. Improving health and safety is not ab out simply giving people checklists and
telling them what to do; it is about letting them know what they need to achieve so that
they can then set about achieving that.
Part 2 of the bill amends the Health and Safety in Employment  Act to provide the
necessary statutory support for the new mini ng regulations. This includes establishing
new classes of duty-holder under the Act, specifically “mine worker” and “mine
operator”. It also includes a definition of the mining operations that will be covered by
the new regulatory regime for mining. This will include all surface and underground
mines and some quarries and tunnels.
Part 2 also provides for enhanced worker  participation arrangements in the mining
industry. The provisions strengthen worker part icipation in health and safety in the
mining industry and, in particular, the f unctions and powers of health and safety
representatives. At the same time it ensures there are appropriate checks and balances to
prevent undue interference in the day-to-day running of mining operations.
All mining operations will be required to have a documented worker participation
system, and this system will cover all mine workers at a site, including contractors and
subcontractors and their employees. The functio ns and powers of site health and safety
representatives will be explicit ly set out in the legislation. These include the ability for
suitably trained representatives to perform in spections and stop operations if there is an
imminent risk of serious harm occurring. Th e bill also establishes a new position of an
industry-wide health and safety representati ve to provide, in the royal commission’s
words, an extra set of eyes and ears and a further line of defence.
These positions can be appointed and f unded either by a union or by another group
of mine workers. The functions and powers of  both site and industr y health and safety
representatives will be balanced by provisions that ensure the health and safety
representatives carry out thei r functions only for health a nd safety purposes, and do not
unnecessarily impede production.
Part 3 of the bill ensures that the legislation that supports the Mines Rescue service is
fit for purpose today. The Mines Rescue se rvice plays a crucial role in emergency
response. The royal commission recommended th at the Mines Rescue Trust Act better
reflect the functions that the service actually carries out, and that there be a review of
the adequacy and fairness of the levy that f unds the service. Part  3 also reflects the
Government’s decision to broaden the respons e to the royal commission to other forms
of mining as well as underground coalmining. It does so by expanding the coverage of
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11375
the Mines Rescue service. The governance of the Mines Rescue Trus t is also amended
to reflect this change in coverage.
The Mines Rescue service has unique expert ise in training and equipping brigades to
respond to emergencies, assisting mine ope rators in emergency preparedness and
deploying brigades, and providi ng advice to mine operators during emergencies. All of
these capabilities will be reflected in the new functions of the Mines Rescue service
provided for in the bill.
The bill also enables the levy that funds the service to be set in regulations. Officials
are currently developing proposals to ensure that the levy adequate ly covers the core
functions of the service while remaining fa ir and proportionate for the mine operators
that will be required to pay it.
The introduction and considera tion of this bill is happening in parallel with public
consultation on the wider package of propos als for the new regulatory regime for
mining. Although the consultation mainly con cerns the proposed mining regulations, it
also covers the worker participation and mines rescue elements of this bill. This parallel
process is necessary to meet the commitmen t to implement the response to the royal
commission’s recommendations by the end of this year.
Submitters have been advised that their submissions on these issues will be taken
into account when officials advise the G overnment and the select committee on any
changes that may be needed to the bill. The public discussion paper also informs likely
submitters of this bill, and invites them to  get involved in the public submission process
on it.
This Government has made a commitment to the families of the victims of the Pike
River mine to ensure that we follow through on every recommendation of the royal
commission. If there can be any good from the tragic loss of lives, then let it be
movement from platitudes to action, and a cr eation of frameworks that will shape better
behaviour and outcomes in the workplace. This b ill is an important step in this process,
and will improve workplace health and safety in the mining sector and beyond in New
Zealand. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I rise to support the referral  of the Health and Safety
(Pike River Implementation) Bill to the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. I
am pleased also to hear that there will be a reasonable process and time to consider what
is a very, very important bill, but is also highly technical when it comes to the mining
regulations.
I want to start by noting again with sadness the needless deaths of the 29 men in that
awful tragedy at Pike River mine. I know th e families will be following this legislation
with great interest, but also it will bring up many of the issues for them again. I know
their lives have been broken by this tragedy. I hope that they have a real opportunity to
meet with the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee and put forward their
views. In fact, the select committee was disc ussing that this morning. I think there is a
willingness by the committee to actually go to them and allow that to happen.
The bill establishes WorkSafe New Zeala nd, which is a stand-alone Crown agency
for workplace health and safe ty. As I said, Labour supports  it, although we have some
reservations that we will wa nt to explore at the select committee.  Secondly, the bill
implements the recommendations around an e ffective regulatory framework for mining.
It makes quite big changes to worker particip ation in health and safety. We want to see
these changes implemented without delay. As I said, the changes to mining are
particularly technical, and, as  the Minister of Labour obser ved, the Safe mines: safe
workers consultation is still incomplete and st ill carrying on, so that needs to feed into
it.
11376 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
It is really important that during the process the workers w ho are expert in the field,
who actually do the jobs, and the people who re present them have real input, and that
those who actually work in mines, quarries , and tunnels are hear d. That is why I am
pleased we have more time. The establishm ent of WorkSafe New Zealand was also the
recommendation of the Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and Safety, which
produced a very comprehensive report. It was a consensus report around the need for
major change in our approach to the health and safety of people at work.
One of the things the taskforce was particularly clear about was the need for tripartite
involvement. It was very clear about that, and in fact the Minister told the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee just 2 week s ago that the WorkSafe board would
include union representation. But we also know, of course, that the Minister is not that
keen. I have seen the Cabinet papers, and there were a few ifs, buts, and maybes.
When we look at the legislation we s ee in clause 7, “Worksafe New Zealand’s
board”, that the Minister must  appoint at least five, but no more than nine, people as
members of the board. It talks about the knowledge and experience required, including
having experience in the public sector, central government processes, and the health and
safety environment, and then there is this  peculiar phrase “perspectives of workplace
participants”. What the heck does that mean ? Is that supposed to be a half-hearted
attempt to include workers and their unions? Could the Minister not bring himself to use
the “u” word in this legislation? If he real ly means it when he talks about tripartism he
should be able to use that word, and it should be very clear in this legislation.
Clause 7 then goes on to talk a bout business generally. The governance
arrangements are left in the hands of the Minister. I am sorry, but on our side of the
House there is not an awful lot of trust in that Minister and in leaving it in his hands.
The perspectives of workplace participants c ould be the perspectives of employers. So
the select committee has to look at that  and demonstrate that it has heard the
Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and Safety and its main recommendation
about the importance of trip artism. That means unions, wo rkers, employers, and the
Government working together, not excludi ng them—not saying: “Oh, they’ve got some
perspectives of workplace participants.” That is a big let-down, and I think there will be
a lot of discussion about that in the select committee.
The functions provided for the WorkSafe New Zealand agency in the bill are a
shadow of those recommended by the task force. The agency has no power to approve
codes of practice. There is no role for it in  making or amending regulations. It has no
clear lead role in workplace health and sa fety. It cannot make recommendations about
the nature of funding. It has no role in fo stering tripartism or working with unions.
Those are significant gaps in the role of this new agency that will need to be addressed
to make this real and to make it work.
What I think we are seeing in this bill is a hanging-on by that Steven Joyce monolith
“MoBIE”—Moby Dick—that was created and was not up to the job, and by those
senior managers who were around when the Pike River mine disaster occurred, who
have not been held to account  for the decisions that le d to that tragedy, who are
desperately trying to cling on to power in that shrinking department.
For goodness’ sake, let us get this agency off on the right foot and accept our history.
Let us understand our history and accept that  the exclusion of workers and workers’
organisations in the health and safety cha nges to legislation in  1992 was a monumental
stuff-up, which ultimately led to the tragedies at Pike River and to those that continue
every week in New Zealand workplaces. Every week people die.
I was reading Subpart 3 of the bill, which is about the transition to WorkSafe New
Zealand. It deals with the transfer of ex isting employees under “MoBIE”—the Ministry
of Business, Innovation and Employment—to  WorkSafe New Zealand. It is very
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11377
interesting because, as I have already pointed  out to the Minister today, the number of
health and safety inspectors will be around half the number we had 2 years ago, and will
be at the lowest level we have had since th e late 1940s. That is how far backwards that
change programme has taken us.
It has been called “lifting our game”, and whether the Minister likes it or not, the
process has been such a botch-up that the inspectors—many of whom have 20 or more
years of experience, and who have been th rough restructuring af ter restructuring—are
calling it “shifting the blame”. I think that is appropriate because nobody at
management level has been held to account for the mess that led to the Pike River mine
disaster. Redundancy notices have been issu ed to some, and inspectors are going down
the road. Trainees will be ta ken on to fill the gap. They will be unwarranted trainees,
and I am told that they are going to be exp ected to do some of the duties of inspectors.
That is really, really concerning.
In my last 2 minutes—there is so much in this bill, and we will get a chance to look
at it—I just want to go back to the point th at I make again and again to this Minister
about work rights and the link between work rights and health and safety, which he does
not get. Obviously, he does not accept that the task force has identified that the health
and safety problems we have in New Zeala nd arose from the deregulation of the labour
market in the 1980s and 1990s. That was the beginning of this. At the same time as we
are considering this bill in the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee we are also
considering a bill that will cut wages, that  could force workers to work longer hours,
and that will cut meal breaks and rest breaks—a fundamental health and safety
entitlement of workers.
We are going to have a big debate about this  bill, but what I woul d like to see as we
progress through this—and we all acknowledge how  important this is—is that we get to
a point where we reach some understanding in  this House that health and safety and
work rights go hand in hand. You cannot have one  without the other. Until this Minister
understands that his weakening of employme nt security and other employment rights
will contribute to health and safety problems, our death toll and injury toll in New
Zealand are going to continue to escalate. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: The significance of this bill, the Health and
Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill, w ill not escape the notice of any members of
this House. I am quite sure of that. I wish to enthusiastically herald its introduction, and
commend it to all parties and all members for th eir attention. The name of the bill, and
of the Act, once passed, carries and conveys the reality and the significance of this piece
of legislation, the Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill. I have said
before in this Chamber that an unforgettable  part of my life is the memory of sitting
through day after day of the testimony hear d by the Royal Commission on the Pike
River Coal Mine Tragedy. I certainly was not alone, but, significantly, I sat in the
company of family, relatives, and friends of the 29 who were lost.
There are four main aspects of  this bill that I wish to jo in the Minister of Labour, the
Hon Simon Bridges, in giving em phasis to. I would like to do that now. First, this bill
acts on the recommendations of the royal commission, establishing a new stand-alone
agency to improve safety in the workpl ace. Second, the bill demonstrates that the
Government and, indeed, I hope, all parties in Parl iament are committed to the Pike
River Implementation Plan. There are 16 reco mmendations from the royal commission
to be implemented by the end of 2013. Third, the Government is committed to
improving workplace safety by specific dates,  with firm targets of a reduction in
workplace fatalities and serious injury. Fourth, the bill needs to be seen by company
directors, public servants, politicians, employers and employees, contractors, and,
indeed, all who are associated with engaging in the workplace not just as a significant
11378 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
step and not just as meeting the require ments of the royal commission, but as an
inexorable, determined drive with the full  weight of parliamentary commitment to
ensure workplace and safety reform. Reform is not an option; it is a commitment and an
essential requirement.
Let us look at some of the sp ecifics. This bill establishes WorkSafe New Zealand as
an independent Crown entity. It amends the Health and Safety in Employment Act 1992
to give new regulations creating clear exp ectations in managing hazards in the mining
industry. It regulates managing those h azards, and it strengthens the minimum
standards. It strengthens th e health and safety manageme nt systems, it provides new
safety-critical roles, it raises training, a nd it increases competency standards. I would
like to give emphasis to the following point—and I can almost hear a cheer down on the
West Coast. It creates the position of check inspectors in mines. It empowers the mines
inspectorate at a greater leve l. It creates a New Zealand Mi ning Board of Examiners. It
allows for the creation of new regulations to be made following the bill’s passage. It
lifts New Zealand to the same  level of standards that m eet best practice throughout the
world.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Let’s not go overboard.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: It creates a Mines Resc ue Act 2013, which will better
reflect the role and functions of the Mines Rescue Trust in providing specialist search
and rescue services in mining emergencie s, training and equipping mines rescue
brigades, providing advice to mine operators during emergencies, and assisting with the
development of emergency plans. I note th e comments of my colleague on the other
side. No, none of this will ha ppen by itself, Mr Little. It will require the full efforts of
everybody involved.
This is not a once-over-lightly bill. This st rikes to the very hear t of the requirements
of the extractive industry. I understand that the Pike River families are being kept
informed of progress towards re-entry of the mine, with all the necessary safety
precautions for doing so, and they are aware that  it will be at leas t a further 3 months
before anything can begin. This bill is not the end of the Pike River mine disaster. This
bill does not give closure for families. It is a continuum for them, and, indeed, for us.
But the families, relatives, and friends of  the 29, the communities of the Coast, and
those committed to winning the benefits of the extractive industries for the rest of us can
be assured that it is a beginning. It is the beginning of a serious reform programme, the
beginning of a commitment, and the beginning of ensuring that we have listened and
learnt, and that we can all look forward to a dding to our visual memorials, adding to the
thoughts of our minds, and adding to the gr ief in our hearts through ensuring the
legislative benefits of learning from the past.
This bill is a continuum in showing that, li ke the fallen in the wa r, the 29 who fell in
the mine disaster will not be forgotten, and we will, and do, remember them. This bill is
a part of the legislative proof that we are determined to look after the interests of those
engaged in mining. It heralds a new beginning  for the extractive i ndustries, and I look
forward to playing a full role, with other me mbers from all sides of the House, in the
select committee process for this. I commend th is bill’s first reading for the unanimous
support of the House. Thank you.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : It is with a sad
heart that I stand to speak on the Health and Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill,
but it is also with some relief. Bill Brazi l, who will be up there somewhere looking
down, spoke to me in 1994 and said prof ound words—post the deregulation of mining
regulations and health and sa fety regulations in 1992—that we  were destined to repeat
the tragedies of the past because we had stepped back from prescriptive mine
regulations developed over 100 years of tr agedies internationa lly, picking up the
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11379
wisdom from each and every one of those trag edies into a set of regulations that took
the best of internati onal knowledge in an attempt to pr otect workers who were always
and who are always working in a unique and usually quite risky en vironment. I say to
Bill that we have finally made the progr ess that you spoke of. Tim Hix was another
miners union delegate whom I worked with —not in a mine but prior to that—whose
death was commemorated 10 years ago last weekend. He was someone who knew of the
dangers and who was passionate about drivi ng change, but, unfortunately, whose life
was taken from him before he could make real progress.
This is a good bill. It is not perfect, a nd I am sure the Transport and Industrial
Relations Committee will deal with it appropriately. There are lessons for each and
every one of us in the passage of this legisl ation. For politicians, it is a lesson for us on
all sides of the House that when we receive advice from officials, we have a
responsibility to ask the hard questions. It is not  good enough to just accept that advice
and move on. If we think there may be so mething wrong, or some deficiency in that
advice, then we should pursue it. I say to th e Ministers over on th e other side of the
House now that they should heed my words,  not because I am full of all wisdom but
because of personal experience and because of watching this sad process since 1992
where Minister after Minister has refused to accept the wisdom of people literally at the
coalface but has accepted the advice of peopl e sitting on their arses in Wellington. Yes,
and I say it with a little bit of anger becau se that is exactly what they were doing:
making judgments on what was right and what  was not right for the safety of people
working underground. It is time we brought check inspectors back  in, people at the
coalface who know what is dangerous and what  is not, not people sitting on their butts
in Wellington. That is what the deregulation brought to the coalmining industry.
It is a lesson for officials. Officials work  under pressure and they do not always have
the resources, so sometimes they make up advice on the best of hints or their
preconceived notions. It is not good enough. If officials know that they do not have the
proper resources to make and provide the proper advice, then they too have to speak up,
because that is exactly what was happening here. Officials sought advice from the big
coalminer, Solid Energy, over a number of years. The big coalminer wanted to get on,
change the culture in the mi ning industry, get rid of all th e old unionists , all the old
miners who had the knowledge, and get a ne w breed of young, keen, energetic miners
who were prepared to work for bonuses, w ho were prepared to forgo some of the
lessons of the past in order to get the coal out of the ground. The lessons for the officials
are to ask more than just the mining comp anies for advice and to seek advice from
everywhere you can.
For company directors there is a lesson here. You may flit around from one company
to another, pollinating the advice from one s ector to another. Being an independent
corporate director is a great honour in this  country. Well, with it comes responsibility.
The people who went to that company, Pike River Coal, looking to get a good return for
the investors had a responsibil ity to make sure that the investment was sound not just
for return to investors but for each and ever y person involved in that project. They did
not. My colleague Andrew Little has taken initi ative to try to address that. The lesson
for company directors is to ask more than just the chief executive officer; ask the people
at the coalface, ask the people in the comp any what is going on, and take responsibility
for your investment and your job.
There is a lesson for the miners. Their enthus iasm to work with one another in risky
environments, to get on and do the job, to gr ow the project, and to deliver incomes for
their families, incomes for their mates, and income for the community is something we
must respect, but it should not be at the expense of safety. Safety should never be
compromised. Some of those miners knew th at things were not right. They were
11380 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
concerned about jobs for their mates. They were concerned about incomes for their own
families. So sometimes, as is human nature, they overlooked the obvious. With best
intents, they ignored some of the lessons of the past and some of the wisdom that was
surrounding them. I am sure there will be many miners—not just the ones at Pike River
but, in fact, those at Spring Creek Mine, wh ere the mine was shut down, effectively, for
6 months after the Pike River disaster because  it too was unsafe. We have to take the
lessons from the past and not forget them.
For the community, for the people on the West Coast, sometimes we place too great
a weight on the individuals who go and do th e jobs to earn the income to provide the
secondary businesses and a nice healthy, vibrant community. We place upon their
shoulders a huge responsibility, and the miners feel that. So perhaps we in the
community expected too much of them, knowi ng full well, in the cas e of Pike River,
that it was a high-risk environment. Relying on an unregulated health and safety system
was not good enough, because human nature and commercial drivers will fail us time
and time again. We know that. I do not think anyone in this House wants to bring in
legislation or regulation unn ecessarily. We do it for good reason most of the time. We
do it to protect ourselves from others, to pr otect ourselves from ourse lves, and to try to
have a community and a working environment that are safe and that can allow people
who go to work to go home at night and look after their families.
The legislation that was changed in 1992 by a National Government that was
determined to deregulate anything it coul d get its hands on was a failure. It was
irresponsible. In fact, we have seen ove r many years deregulation being called the
panacea to all economic woes—the way forward. Well, this was a sad and tragic
experiment. I acknowledge the work and the commitment by this National Government
to put back into place some prescriptive legislation for underground coalmining. It is
necessary. Bill Brazil told me that in 1994. He was right. I take some responsibility.
Should I have shouted and screamed from th e rooftops? Should I have marched in the
streets to get the legislati on changed? Perhaps I should ha ve, but it is in cumbent upon
this House here, each and ever y one of us, to not buy into th is ideology that says that
less regulation, a hands-off Government, and hands-off regulation ar e going to protect
each and every one of us. There are some people who work in risky environments and
there are some people who are less able th an others who need protection. It is the
responsibility of this House and of any G overnment to put in place those necessary
protections.
Today we are introducing into the Hous e the Health and Safety (Pike River
Implementation) Bill. Can I acknowledge Bernie Monk, Nick Davidson, the families,
and the people who were determined to push ahead to have a proper inquiry in order to
understand what went on here and then to ensu re that change occurred. This is the start
of that change, and we commit to follow it through for better mining safety.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: T ēnā koe. Can I begin with the unusual step of
acknowledging my colleagues from West Co ast - Tasman, Chris Auchinvole and the
Hon Damien O’Connor, and congratulate them both on two excellent speeches.
In the 1980s and 1990s New Zealand experi enced a wave of change, underpinned by
the boneheaded notion that if a Government takes a hands-off attitude to more or less
everything, then the free-market competition that results between unregulated
companies will somehow magically produce the best outcomes for everyone. The
theory was applied not only to goods and serv ices but also to whole industries and areas
of core public services, like electricity ge neration, health, and education. One of the
casualties of this enthusiasm for deregul ation was leaky homes. Ordinary people
became the victims of corner-cutting and but t-covering by all those who could now get
away with it. The same thing happened with finance companies.
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11381
Another casualty was safety  in underground mines. In 1992 the Government threw
away the prescriptive mine safety rules th at had been built up by the experience of
centuries—many years—underground. These ru les were eventually replaced with
requirements that mining companies take safety  measures that are “practicable”. That
requirement has embedded in it affordability , because a company that cannot afford a
particular safety measure will not find it to be  practicable, with the result that different
mines will have different safety standards. At the same time, the “triangle of safety”, as
Dave Feickert refers to representatives of companies, workers, and Government, who all
have responsibility for safety, was demolishe d with the abolition of check inspectors
and then a radical downgrad e of the Government’s mine s inspectorate. Thus the
National Government in the 1990s first of al l radically weakened the actual rules for
underground mine safety, and then dismantled the structures to monitor and enforce
compliance.
None of these changes was reversed by Labour in its years of Government, and
throughout all of that time experts warned that that erosion of safety would result in the
loss of life. It did in 2006 and then agai n in 2010. In 1995 in hi s submission to the
inquiry into the administration of occupati onal safety and health policy, coalmining
safety expert Bill Brazil, whom the Hon Damien O’Connor has already referred to, said:
“Furthermore the [Health and Safety in Employment] Act is being used as a
manipulative device to eliminate management  structures and many historically formed
mining codes of practice that were firmly  established in the heart of previous
legislation, much of which ha s proved successful over 100 year s. Should th is situation
be allowed to continue without intervention the end result can only be the escalation of
potential for further disaster.” How right he was.
From my kitchen window I look out at the Paparoas, where 29 men still lie. I am
reminded every day of my commitment that those men’s remains are brought back to
their families, that the investigation of thei r deaths sees justice done, and that systems
are reconstructed to protect all other underground miners from avoidable risk. Mine was
one of the very first calls for a royal commissi on of inquiry into the Pike River tragedy.
Then I came to this House day after day, pressing the Minister of Labour to reinstate the
mines inspectorate and overhaul the health and safety regulatory framework, until the
Government eventually capitulated, created the High Hazards Unit, and established the
Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health and Safety. The royal commission and the
independent task force both produced excellent recommendations.
I would like to say that the job of recons tructing those safety systems to protect
miners is now being completed with this bill, the Health and Safety (Pike River
Implementation) Bill, but I cannot. When the Government said it would implement all
of the recommendations of the royal commission, I cautiously welcomed the
announcement but said the devil would be in th e detail. Now we have seen some of the
detail, and it has become clea r that the Government intends a pale facsimile of what the
royal commission and the independent task fo rce intended. Of course we welcome the
Government’s eventual acceptance that a st and-alone occupational safety and health
agency is required. But rather than the very  strong tripartite model recommended by the
royal commission and strongly endorsed by the independent task force, the Government
instead proposes, as Darien Fenton has alr eady commented, the vague formulation that
the Minister will have regard to the perspectives of workplace participants, as one of six
general criteria for appointing board members.
The functions of the new entity owe much more to the standoffi sh, half-hearted and
proven inadequate approach of  the Department of Labour to  these responsibilities than
to the strong, authoritative, and proactive agency that had been intended. The agency
will enforce the legislation, but every othe r function—and there are 13 functions—is to
11382 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
advise, promote, provide guidance, and genera lly give the appearance of action without
authority. The Government is proceeding to provide for advisory groups when this has
been resoundingly rejected by participants in the task force process, particularly as it
seems that this will be accompanied by th e dismantling of the Workplace Health and
Safety Council. I invite subsequent Government speakers to tell me if I am wrong, but if
I am right, such a dismantling would seem  to contravene International Labour
Organization conventions, to which New Zealand is signatory.
The changes in Part 2 of th e bill certainly go part-way towards re-establishing that
triangle of safety I referred to earlier, and I am pleased that it is largely based on the
Queensland Coal Mining Safety and Health Act. In a variety of places, however, the bill
resorts again to weasel words. For example,  in the proposed new section 19Q in clause
27, which is pivotal, mine opera tors must show that there is “a documented worker
participation system that provides reasona ble opportunities for the mine workers to
participate” in improving health and safety. I want to state categorically that that is not
enough. Successful mine safety programmes require that there is full worker
participation. It can never be acceptable under the law for an employer to be able to say:
“Well, we provided them the opportunity but they didn’t show up at the meeting.”
I remain profoundly disappointed that the G overnment has not moved to address the
“all practicable steps” formulation in the Ac t itself. More prescrip tive regulations for
mining should emerge from the new processes being established, but unless the problem
is dealt with in the Act, I believe it will continue to drive haphazard practice in
industries such as forestry, which also has an appalling safety recor d. Part 3 of the bill
establishes a wider role and sounder footing fo r the Mines Rescue service, and that is
long overdue. The pity is that the Governme nt’s woeful management of Solid Energy
and its current underground coalmines may ha ve already meant a critical loss of
expertise from our Mines Rescue service.
All in all, one has the impression that th e Government has not learnt its lesson and
again hoped to get away with superficial or  half-hearted adjustment, rather than the
fundamental change that is called for. On 22 November 2010 John Key said: “I have no
reason to believe that New Zealand’s safety standards are any less than Australia’s, and
in fact our safety record for the most part  has been very good”. He has since denied in
this House that deregulation was at the heart of the systems failure that allowed the Pike
River tragedy to occur, and one has the impression with this bill that the Government is
responding to public perception rather than a genuine understanding of the need for
fundamental change. We will support this bill at this stage, we will follow the
submissions with very close interest, and we w ill need there to be significant change to
continue to support it.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I would like to congratulate the
Minister of Labour, the Hon Simon Bridge s, on bringing through to the House the
Health and Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill. As many members of this House
have said, and, I am sure, further speeches will indicate, this bill relates to a very serious
tragedy in our country’s history. We wish to pa y tribute to those lost in that tragedy and
also to their families and the wider commun ity of that region. To all those who are
involved in the productive industries of New Zealand, in forestry, in mining, and in
agriculture, where lives are at risk because of the nature of thos e industries, it is
difficult. That is something we need to be ve ry aware of and cognisant of in this House,
to make sure that we take the best approach possible.
I would just like to pay tribute to the local  MPs from that area, Chris Auchinvole and
Damien O’Connor, who have spoken in this House, and their words. They, as local
members, will have been touched immensely by the events that happened there. We
look forward to their contributions through th ese debates. We look forward also to the
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11383
contributions of the political parties involved in the process. We are very fortunate to
have on the Transport and Industrial Rela tions Committee members who have a good
awareness of labour relations law and re gulations, and we look forward to their
involvement in making sure that we get the best possible result.
I guess the only disappointing part has been the Green Party and its last speech. This
is not something, I think, for which anybody ca n attribute blame. It is a very difficult
situation. We hope that the Green Party will be constructive in the way that it works
within the committee towards getting the best  results for New Zealanders, our industry,
and, especially, those people who put themselves at most risk day by day working in our
very dangerous productive industries. Thank you.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: New Zealand First will be supporting the
Health and Safety (Pike River Implementation)  Bill. We welcome the changes that this
bill will make to our mining sector. Health and safety is absolutely essential in this
particular workplace. New Zealand First agreed with the report of the Royal
Commission on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy, and we are happy to now see that
many of its recommendations have been heard and are being implemented. The Pike
River tragedy, as we all know, cannot be blamed  on just one factor but resulted from a
series of errors. It is very sad that it took this devastating tragedy and 29 lives to make
the changes necessary to improve  the health and safety regulations in the mining sector
happen. New Zealand First acknowledges the families and friends of those lost in the
Pike River tragedy and all of  those other people caught up in this disaster who are
dealing with and dealt with this particul ar tragedy. And, of course, we need to
acknowledge the two West Coast MPs as well, the Hon Damien O’Connor and Chris
Auchinvole.
We are very pleased to see the workplac e agency, WorkSafe New Zealand, that is
being created under this particular bill. The intention of this agency is to improve
workplace health and safety through the creat ion of a stand-alone health and safety
agency that will have a dedicated focus on health and safety. We were very impressed
when we had a look at clause 10, on the Work Safe agency’s functions. It appears to be
quite a thorough list. At the Transport a nd Industrial Relations Committee we will
examine these very thoroughly. But we want action with authority when it comes to
these particular issues.
In 1998 New Zealand First voted for the Mi nistry of Energy (Abolition) Amendment
Bill (No 2). In doing so, we were advocati ng for a centralised agency that would be
responsible for all things that  related to health  and safety. We believed then and we
believe now that a sole Government agency ought to have centralised responsibility for
ensuring that responsible health and safety  practices are undertaken in every workplace
in New Zealand. It has been a very unfortunate  fact that successive Governments either
underfunded the Department of Labour, resul ting in very few health and safety
inspectors, or allowed the Department of Labour to underfund the mining inspectorate,
for which it was responsible—a disaster just waiting to happen. When one goes to work
in the morning, there is the inherent expecta tion that one will return  home safely after a
day’s work, and that health and safety re quirements in the workplace have been
complied with to ensure that this actually happens.
The bill also provides amendments to th e Health and Safety in Employment Act
1992. This change will see new, clear mining regulations such as processes for better
managing hazards, increasing minimum standards, requirements for health and safety
standards, and strengthened training a nd competency requirements. The royal
commission’s focus on this was for a mos tly underground mine. However, the changes
in this bill will focus on all mining operations , due to the hazards that they actually
present. New Zealand First has always supported an increase in health and safety
11384 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
regulations for our workers. We are also aw are, too, that the unions have voiced their
concerns around this particular issue. Duri ng the select committee process we need to
review whether or not the unions can be i nvolved in checking out the credentials of
some of these health and safety inspec tors. We look forward to hearing their
submissions, and many others, through the se lect committee process, and we believe
that each and every one of them needs to be taken into serious  consideration. We
support changes to health and safety, and we  look forward to the contributions from
others on this committee.
The royal commission found that  the effectiveness of th e mines inspectorate had
been declining for many years, and by the time of the tragedy the Department of
Labour, unfortunately, had onl y two mining inspectors. Basically, this was totally
insufficient for New Zealand. They were unabl e to discharge their statutory functions.
In short, in whichever form, old or new, th e deterioration of the mines inspectorate was
an inevitable consequence of political neglect after 1998. While undertaking that task, it
also decided to integrate the mines inspectorate, a leftover aspect of the Ministry of
Energy residing in the Ministry  of Commerce, into the larger Occupational Safety and
Health Service within the Department of Labour. Questions were raised about this from
both sides of the House, regarding how the newly transferred mines inspectorate would
actually be funded. It is also worthy of not e that well and truly before the Pike River
tragedy, the Opposition had raised questions about th e adequacy of the mines
inspectorate. We know that several mine insp ectors had lost their jobs in transfers and
were paid out redundancy accordingly. Many of these positions were not refilled and, as
outlined in the report, that left only two in spectors. This in itself was a recipe for
disaster.
We know, having read through the royal commission report, that there were a
number of safety issues at Pike River th at went totally unaddressed. Failure across a
number of Government departments and sections of Pike River management
contributed to this tragedy. This is a view that we believe is advocated in the royal
commission report, where it explains the Swiss cheese model of causation, where it is
maintained that there needs to be a perfect storm of failings across agencies, coupled
with human error, before an accident on this scale can actually occur.
We welcomed the royal commission repor t on this tragedy, and we now welcome
this bill to implement changes to improve the sector; they are ve ry much needed. New
Zealand First will be supporting this bill to make these much-needed improvements.
Safety should never ever be compromised, particularly in the mining industry. This
legislation is absolutely essential and we look forward to working on it.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am pleased to take a call on this bill, the
Health and Safety (Pike River Implementatio n) Bill, and I want to join with other
members of the House in acknowledging, and paying tribute to, those fine men who lost
their lives as a result of the Pike River tragedy. I do that knowing that words will never
really adequately express the sort of anguish and loss that  occurs in these sorts of
events, but I do so in a manner that suggests th at in terms of life a nd its cruel outcomes
and tragedies, often we have to look rearward  to learn what to do next. In that sense,
there are really no “what ifs”; there are just lessons to be learnt, and this bill is very
much about what is next.
In acknowledging the lives lost, I also want  to acknowledge the families that remain
behind and the role that they themselves and others around them may play in the select
committee process. I want to also acknowledge Damien O’Connor and Chris
Auchinvole—members from the affected area of Pike River—and the steadfast support
that I know they have provided to those involved.
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11385
This bill is an omnibus bill. It really does recognise many of the lessons learnt, and it
reflects the findings of the r oyal commission of inqui ry. I just want to  briefly touch on
the three main spokes that the bill is dealing with. Firstly, it establishes WorkSafe New
Zealand, a Crown agency that essentially st arts a new health and safety agency. To
some extent, I think we can all have some degree of scepticism inasmuch as, actually,
workplace health and safety is not about just the structure that sits above the workplace,
the chief executive officer, the supervisor s within the workplace, or the workers
themselves; it is a combination of all those factors, and, in some circumstances, as
Barbara Stewart, the member who has just re sumed her seat, recognises, a perfect storm
will work against all those things at play. But this is about ensuring that the legislative
framework that is being worked through here does as much as possible to ensure that all
the relevant components are lined up.
The second part of the bill contains the amen dments that will be made to the Health
and Safety in Employment Act and the new re gulatory regime that sets out some clear
expectations in terms of hazard management. The third limb of th e bill creates a new
Act called the Mines Rescue Act. A number have commented on the circumstances that
have led to this. I very much want to encour age us now to think about what is next and
the way in which we, as members of Parlia ment, can support not only workers within
this industry but workers across New Zeal and in constructing the best legislative
framework we can for their health and safety  and for the health and safety of their
families. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I rise to speak on the Health and Safety (Pike River
Implementation) Bill, and in acknowledgment of  the last speaker, Mr Sabin, I just say
that I do not think the families or the miners who continue to mine in this country today
and their communities, and the unions to whic h those miners belong, expect this House
to continue to come up with comforting words to continue to ease the grief and the loss.
What they do expect is this House to come  up with meaningful and genuine action that
genuinely takes account of the now studied failu res and gaps in the system that led to
the Pike River tragedy.
The Government and the Minister of La bour, the Hon Simon Bridges, and, indeed,
Chris Finlayson before him as the Acting Minister of Labour, and Kate Wilkinson
before him, who was the Minister of Labour in office at the time of this tragedy, are
entitled to the gratitude of the House for bringing this important bill to the House at this
time. As we all know, it follows the roya l commission and its study of the dreadful
disaster. The Pike River coalmine tragedy was the worst industrial disaster in more than
40 years, and we now know, and we need not  be ashamed or feel  guilty about it any
more, that it was the product of poor regulation, poor oversight and inspection, and poor
governance and management.
The royal commission was very clear. The Health and Safety in Employment Act
1992 was, at that time, half-baked and a half  measure. We have le arnt that lesson. We
have been told that. Even the subsequent attempts by the Labour Government to fix it
up—good attempts and the correct efforts to be made—were not enough to make it a
robust and enduring, but ultimately safe, piece of legislation. We have made the mistake
before. We made it in 1992. Let us not make the mistake again. This is not about just
the Pike River 29, and we do not honour just the Pike River 29 with this bill and getting
it right. There are the three miners who died on the West Coast in 1998, the one down in
Ōhai in 2003, the one in 2006, and now the Pike River 29 in 2010.
This bill is an opportunity to set a new standard for health and safety in all
workplaces, for all employers, and for the bene fit of all workers in New Zealand. This
bill is a chance, a first step, to honour thos e dying on our farms, in our fisheries, on our
construction sites, and in our forests. I acknowledge the work of Helen Kelly of the
11386 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
Council of Trade Unions on her campaign on forest ry safety. This bill is a first step and
a first chance to honour people like Ken Callo w of the East Coast and Adam Olsson of
Taranaki. This bill is largely confined to the mining industry, and that is a good industry
to start with, given its track record.
Although we support the bill at this stage, we are saying it is a good first draft, and
that is all it is. It beefs up the inspectorat e and it creates WorkSafe. It is explicit about
worker participation, and it provides for indus try health and safety inspectors, which is
the check inspector that certainly the union and its members in mining have been calling
for for many years. I first made the call fo r check inspectors in 2004, and made it again
in 2005 and 2006—and so it went on—in my capacity as union secretary.
But let us not forget about the reality of workplace relationships and employment
agreements. Workplace relationships and employment agreements are about a
relationship of power and control. That is something else we should not feel ashamed of
or guilty about admitting. That is the reality. It  is the legal reality, and it is the practical
reality. The employer has ultimate control. Th e worker has a duty of  obedience. That is
how the workplace works. But health and safe ty risks, hazards at work, and danger at
work directly affect workers. It is work ers who are the ones who are killed and maimed
when poor health and safety happens at work. It is not management; it is workers. Input
by workers into health and safety and risk assessment and risk management must be real
and genuine. Their voice, the worker voice, must be genuine and meaningful.
The royal commission of inquiry into the Pike  River tragedy went to great lengths to
underscore the need for worker input. It talk ed about tripartitism, and so did the recent
Independent Taskforce on Workplace Health  and Safety. They both underscored the
need for worker input, and they said that tripartitism must start from the top. So we
should expect to see it in the governance of WorkSafe, we should expect to see it in the
governance of Mines Rescue, and we should expect to see it in the health and safety
measures, in the governance measures, in th e workplace, at the enterprise level—not
with the directors, although they  need to be aware of it, bu t in the way that health and
safety is given oversight at the enterprise.

items.speaker: Here is the thing
items.text: this bill, if  it is to be effective, if it is to honour the Pike River 29
and everyone else who has died unnecessarily at work since 1992, will have to tell
employers what to do. It will have to be instructive and mandatory. We must honour the
call for a better, stronger voice for workers in  health and safety in our mines and in
every workplace. Even when some employers turn up to this Parliament to quibble and
cavil, this House should not quail from legislati ng as far as is nece ssary to protect and
preserve life and limb in the workplace. That is our duty. Anything less is negligent, and
that is what we on this side of the Hous e will be going into this deliberative process
with as our objective.
Some aspects of this bill in its first draft do not come up to specification. For
example, new section 13AA in clause 25, which deals with the training and supervision
of mine workers, talks about employers taking “al l practicable steps”  to ensure that
mine workers have been properly trained and are properly superv ised. That is not
adequate. It is not enough to take all practicable steps; it must be a requirement that
miners employed to do the dangerous work  of mining, especially underground mining,
have the proper training and qualifications and are provided with the proper supervision.
New section 19Q in clause 27, “General duty to involve mine workers in health and
safety matters”, simply requires, as pr esently drafted, “reasona ble opportunities” for
input. That is not enough. That will not be e nough. If this bill comes back to this House
with that language still in it, we will not have done our job and the bill will not come up
to the mark.
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11387
New section 19R talks about the development of worker participation systems, and it
is there where we must be absolutely on our mettle to ensure that the worker voice is
properly provided for and will be heard. Engagement between management and workers
over health and safety must be real, an d it must be prot ected and supported by
legislation. We do not need legislative skeuomorphism.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Skeuomorphism.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: We do not need a bill that looks like it is doing one thing, but
is actually doing another. I see that Dr Cald er is taken with the language, and that is
good. He can go into the deliberative process in his caucus when the bill comes back for
endorsement and ask the question of the chai r of the select committee and, indeed, of
the Minister: “Do we still have a bill th at is just another piece of legislative
skeuomorphism, or do we have a real bill th at will have real effects and will provide
real protection?”.
Barbara Stewart talked about one of the findings of the royal commission being the
Swiss cheese model of failure and disaster. Well, we need to go from the Swiss cheese
model to the Swiss Army knife model. We need to go to a health and safety legislative
framework that provides all necessary protections, respects the role of management, and
provides proper protection for workers, be cause nothing less will do. We have had the
lesson—the bitter, cold, hard lesson. We have  seen what bad legislation does. We can
avoid it if we are on our mettle and perform our duty, and we are here to do that.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: There have been some very thoughtful
contributions from all sides of the House on this piece of legisl ation, the Health and
Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill. Tangiwai, Wahine, Christchurch, Pike River—
tragedies seared into our nation’s collective consciousness. I want to acknowledge those
lost at Pike River and the continued pain and suffering of the loved ones left behind,
who will continue to mourn their loss as long as they are alive.
We are committed as a Government to our Pike River Implementation Plan. This is
an omnibus bill that enacts the recommenda tions of the Royal Commission on the Pike
River Coal Mine Tragedy. It  establishes WorkSafe Ne w Zealand, which is a new
workplace health and safety agency, it ame nds the Health and Safety in Employment
Act 1992, and it creates a new Mines Rescue Act 2013.
The Pike River Implementation Plan has 16 recommendations a nd we are aiming to
have these implemented by the end of this year. National is committed as a Government
to improving workplace safety across the board, and so we have set a firm target for
ourselves of having a 25 percent reduction in the rate of workplace fatalities and serious
injuries by 2020. This is a significant step in the Government’s workplace health and
safety reform programme. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand the ne xt call is a split
call—5 minutes.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Can I also start my contribution to the debate on this
bill, the Health and Safety (Pike River Implementation) Bill, by acknowledging the 29
men who died in the Pike River mine tragedy and their families. They suffered from
losing one of the most fundamental rights at work: the fundamental right to walk out the
door in the morning, go to work, do your job, and return home safely to your loved
ones. Sadly, for far too many New Zealand workers, including the 29 at Pike River
mine, that has not happened. The fact that  that has not happened is a blight on our
country and on our country’s laws, and that is what we are attempting to resolve today.
But can I say at the outset that, yes, we have learnt a lesson. Can we please never
ever forget it? History is sometimes there to repeat itself, and this is one piece of history
that must never repeat itself. We must  never have to relearn the lesson about
deregulation of the workforce and in the wo rkplace and the traged ies that it actually
11388 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013
leads to, because, to me, that is the lesson of  Pike River mine and other tragedies. They
were not things that were accidents. They did not just happen. They were designed to
happen and they happened through poor design. That is what the royal commission told
us. We must never unlearn that lesson again.
In a decade’s time, I do not want to ever hear any parliamentarian in this House
argue for deregulation in the workplace, because today we are accepting right across
parties, I think, unanimously in  the House, that deregulation risks health and safety for
workers. I expect that if everyone is genui ne about their commitments to this debate,
they are accepting that premise. If they are accepting that premise, then can I say to the
Government that it cannot happen in isolation. It  is not just one bill that needs to accept
that reality. It is, in fact, all of the employ ment legislation before this House that needs
to understand that reality. To accept just in th is bill and not in ot hers that deregulation
risks workers’ health and safety is to pay lip-service to learning the lessons of the Pike
River mine tragedy and other tragedies.
I say this because earlier today I was on the Transpor t and Industrial Relations
Committee and we were debating and discussing  another piece of legislation before the
House, on employment rights. That piece of  legislation does further deregulate the
workplace.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: No, it’s not this bill.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is not this bill, and that is my point, Mr Sabin. It is not OK to
recognise that deregulation is a bad thing just  when it comes to this bill. It actually
needs to be right across the board because the bill, Mr Sabin, that we were discussing
actually reduces workers’ rights to—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Yeah, it’s not this bill—that’s my point.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: My point, Mr Sabin is that it ac tually reduces workers’ rights to
having a lunch break and rest periods. That is  a fundamental health and safety issue.
That the members opposite do not seem to get that gives me no comfort, because they
can pass this bill and think they have done their job, but if they continue to deregulate
other parts of the workplace, they ar e not honouring—they are not honouring—the
lesson that needs to be learnt from Pike River mine and those other tragedies. They need
to be serious about this, not just with this piece of legislation but with every single piece
of legislation that they currently have before this Parliament that attempts to deregulate
the workplace. I am proud to stand and support this bill and I urge the Government to
take this issue seriously with regard to other pieces of legislation.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to speak on behalf of the Greens for this bill, the
Health and Safety (Pike River Implementati on) Bill. The bill enacts some of the
recommendations from the Royal Commissi on on the Pike River Coal Mine Tragedy,
an inquiry that was pushed for by the Green s—and we are certainl y glad that it was
carried out. The commission’s report into th e tragedy, where 29 men lost their lives,
highlighted the areas where we could be doing a lot better to provide safe workplaces so
that those men, and other people like them, can come home from work.
There were 16 recommendations in the report.  The bill deals with some of them but
not all of them. The Greens will be supporting this bill. We recognise that health and
safety regulation in this country is l ong overdue and it is time we focused on a
framework that puts the safety of workers be fore the profits of bus iness. It has been
acknowledged that the loss of lives at Pike River was the result of a series of actions and
inactions, culture, and a health and safety fr amework that lacked the appropriate checks
and balances. So it is heartening to see some remedies in this bill.
We support the creation of WorkSafe New Z ealand. We believe that an independent
agency that has, as its main focus, health and safety, and that is charged with education,
monitoring, and compliance, will provide  some safeguards. I note that around $34
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11389
million has been allocated to the creation of this agency in the last Budget round. This
has even had the Employers and Manufacturer s Association quite co ncerned that that
may not be enough to adequately resource and staff an agency so that it can fulfil its
compliance and monitoring work. We support th e introduction of stronger regulations,
and we recognise that this bill is a step towards encouraging worker participation and
highlighting safety breaches and hazards. We welcome the provisions that create
workplace health and safety representatives who have the power to suspend operations
if there is serious concern for harm.
But what we need is a shift in culture so that workers and contractors and staff in any
mine are able to speak up if they are worri ed about safety. We know that we will see
that shift in unionised workplaces. The research shows that where there is a strong
union presence, workers are safer because they can speak up. This is not the case in the
forestry sector, a deregulate d industry where workers are is olated from each other and
that has low union membership. This fear of  speaking up is exactly what happened at a
public meeting on forestry that  I was at last week in Gi sborne, with my colleague
Darien Fenton from Labour. None of the worker s in the 50 or so people in the crowd
said a word, because there were bosses there—and they certainly spoke up.
We recognise that this bill is quite a dramatic change from the original 1992 Health
and Safety in Employment Act, which intr oduced the deregulated framework for health
and safety. This Act replaced other legislati on in the mining industry that ensured that
there was independent monitoring and complian ce with health and sa fety standards in
mines—my colleague Kevin Hague has talk ed about that. The 1992 Act ushered in a
concept of the cost-benefit analysis being taken with workplace hazards. Employers
were urged to take practicable steps to minimise and isolate hazards, but only if they
could afford to do so. I note that there was a draft code of practice in the mining sector
that remained in draft form until 2006.
So it is a huge step forw ard to have WorkSafe New Zealand and some provisions for
the voice of workers, but if we want safe  workplaces across New Zealand, not just in
mines, the Government must stop undermin ing unions and removing the ability for
workers to bargain collectively. It needs to shift away from the truly awful amendments
it is making to the Employment Relations Act and it needs to positively encourage
workers to speak up and join their unions.
We are looking forward to examining this bill more closely as it goes through the
select committee process, but in the meantime we commend this bill to the House.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): I am pleased to stand in support of this
first reading of the Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill. As I think I
have said in the House severa l times before, context is im portant. I firstly, therefore,
join with colleagues around th e House in acknowledging the context of the Pike River
coalmine and the tragedy there that has facilitated the approach of this bill in the House.
Secondly, this area of safety is always some thing that is constantly evolving. As those
who have spoken before me have noted, this  is a bill of three parts dealing with
everything from the mines to an omnibus aspe ct, and to the establishment of WorkSafe
New Zealand. I commend this bill to the House.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee.

(Pike River Implementation) Bill be reported back to the House on or before 30 October
