11390 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I move, That the
Psychoactive Substances Bill be now read a second time . I want to thank the Health
Committee for its thoughtful consideration of  this bill and also the many people who
made submissions on this important piece of legislation. I appreciate your broad support
for, and the helpful comments on, the detail of the bill. Because of the overwhelming
wish of New Zealanders for the Government to act on the sale and use of psychoactive
substances, so-called legal hi ghs, the committee has had a s horter period than usual to
consider this bill. I greatly appreciate  the cross-party suppor t that has enabled
Parliament to expeditiousl y deal with this issue. The shortened time frame was
recognition of the significant problem that unregulated psychoactive substances have
become and the need to find a solution.
I would like to take a moment to acknowledge the considerable amount of work done
by the Hon Peter Dunne in getting this bill to  this stage. The Hon Peter Dunne has been
a driving force behind this world-first legisl ation, and we need to  recognise the great
work that has been put in place by Mr Dunne in this area.
It is worth taking the time to remind ourselv es what this bill is about. This bill is
squarely about safety. It was prompted by concerns about untested substances being
sold with no controls. The Government c ould have banned indivi dual substances once
we found out what they were, but this process was reactive and extremely time-
consuming. For each banned substance th e Government had to identify what the
substance was and identify possible harm fr om it before any action could be taken.
Unfortunately the realities of living in th is technological age meant that there were
always new ones waiting with the potentia l to cause more harm. The number of
substances available, potentially thousands, meant this was ne ver going to be more than
a temporary fix.
This bill will fix this problem once and fo r all. No longer will the onus be on the
Government to show a risk of harm; the onus will be on anyone wanting to produce a
psychoactive product to show it  poses no more than a low risk of harm. In order to do
that, there must be a way in which producer s can demonstrate that their product meets
the standard. But even if pr oducts meet that standard, th e Government will still be
insisting on tight controls around their availability. For starters, from day one of
enactment, neighbourhood dairies will no longer be entitled to stock any such product,
nor will sales to those under 18 years of ag e be permitted. These restrictions were
always the Government’s intention, but I a ppreciate the Health Committee’s wish to
have that detailed in the primary register—legislation rather than regulations.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: It always pays to read the speech beforehand. It always pays
to read it through and you can work out the big words that way.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: Yes, Mr Mallard. Lots of thi ngs always pay, but thanks for
the advice. These and other restrictions, in cluding restricting where advertising can
occur, provide absolute certainty that the G overnment is serious about controlling these
substances and preventing harm.
Other changes made in the select comm ittee include some clarification of the
principle and purpose of this bill. The ne w version of the bill clarifies that the
legislation is about protecting the health of  individuals who use these substances. The
select committee also inserted a principle th at a product that meets a standard will be
approved. If there really  are products that meet these te sts and pose only a low risk of
harm, then they will be approved. This bill was never meant to be a ban by stealth; it is
about providing safer communities for our young people in particular.
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11391
One issue on which there was a great deal of discussion was the offences provision in
the bill. On balance the Government reco mmended keeping the offences for possession
of an unapproved product and possession of  any psychoactive substance by people
under 18. I know that a lot of submitters want ed no personal possession offence, and I
respect that view. Submitters raised a concern, in particular, about young people having
their future travel and employment opti ons blighted through yout hful foolishness. I
agree that this would be an undesirable outcome. This bill is not about establishing a
new class of criminal, but I do not think reco gnising that there still needs to be some
personal responsibility taken is a bad thing. However, I can assure those who argued
against a personal possession prov ision that we have very carefully made sure no one
will receive a criminal conviction simply by possessing one of these substances. The
worst thing that can happen is an infringeme nt notice similar to a speeding ticket. I am
assured by police that even this would be a last resort. The fi rst response will be
education and possibly referral to  health or social services . These provisions will allow
police to intervene and pr event harm to young people and harm from unapproved
substances—the harm that I talk ed about earlier, and the harm  that this bill is intended
to prevent.
Another issue raised was the impact of these products on local communities. The
select committee heard very strong submissions from local authorities on this issue in
particular. In response, the bill now contai ns provisions allowing local authorities to
restrict outlet locations  and density, similar to the provi sions in the Sale and Supply of
Alcohol Act.
The final issue that I want to talk about is  that of animal testing. I know that this is
an issue that many, if not most, people feel very strongly about. Let me say now that I
respect those feelings and I share them. If th ere are suitable non-anim al tests, then they
must and will be used. This bill is a response to the harm  caused by untested products,
and the countervailing consideration must be human safety. We must be sure that the
tests that these products are put  through give us robust inform ation so that the regulator
can make sound decisions. Whether or not there is a suitable non-animal test is a matter
for the experts.
The Ministry of Health established an interim expert committee, including experts on
toxicology, pharmacology, and animal welfar e. Mr Dunne asked that committee for
advice on non-animal tests, clearly articula ting his strong preference for a regime that
excluded animal testing. The committee’s advice was that some animal testing would be
necessary at first to ensure that the ri sk of products was accurately assessed. The
committee went on to advise that there were some alternative tests that could be used
immediately, and that it would continue to work to identify other alternatives.
After receiving this advice I asked the Health Committee to consider an amendment
to the bill that would put controls on an imal testing, and put a duty on the expert
advisory committee to actively seek alterna tives. I am very plea sed to say that the
committee members agreed unanimously to these amendments, which are in clause 11A
of the revised bill. The expert advisory committee will actively seek alternatives to
animal tests, and, again, I want to make it clear that there will be no animal testing
where there is a suitable alternative. The ove rriding principle remains the need to make
sure that the products sold in New Zealand pose no more than a low risk of harm. The
importance of that principle is why this bill is before the House.
This bill is also timely, as I moved, as a new Minister, to refresh the National Drug
Policy. Although there will be separate discus sions and consultations held to discuss
what else can be done in this area, starti ng with a discussion forum tomorrow hosted by
the New Zealand Drug Foundation, the restri ctions placed on psychoactive substances
11392 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
through this bill will form an important co mponent of New Zealand’s policy on drugs
for the future.
I am aware that drug policy is a particular ly polarising area, and I have no doubt that
in the course of the National Drug Policy’s de velopment a variety of interested parties
will float a wide range of ideas , many of which may not be a cceptable to me or to this
Government. However, if thinking outsi de the box achieves even one promising
proposal that will reduce the dependency and harm that come from drug use, then I
believe that it is worth the effort.
Ensuring that we do not have high-risk, novel psychoactive substances on shop
shelves is the purpose of the bill, and it w ill be achieved with this legislation. I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak in the second reading of the Psychoactive Substances Bill. Can I welcome the
new Minister, Todd McClay, to the debate on this issue, an d can I suggest to him that
the process and the thinking behind this piece of legislation were far superior than for
some of the legislation that he promoted in  the House as a private member. I hope he
learns from this experience, because this is the way to go, Minister. I really also—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s not a high test.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is not a high test, no. I also ought to recognise the
Hon Peter Dunne, who is the ar chitect of this legislation, who steered it through its first
stages in the House, and who steered it from its genesis as a set of recommendations out
of the Law Commission report to becoming legi slation. It is good to see Peter Dunne in
the House this evening.
Can I say thank you very much to colleagues on the Health Committee. I have to say,
barring a couple of process issues—and I do n eed to reflect on thos e—the constructive
approach that all members of the select  committee took to this legislation was
encouraging. It is the sort of thing that I wish the New Zealand public could actually get
to see more often. I want to acknowledge part icularly Paul Hutchison and Scott
Simpson from the National Party side, who rea lly worked hard to improve this bill. I
think it has come back to the House in much be tter shape than it was in when it went to
the select committee.
I did say there were a couple of process i ssues, and I do need to just briefly reflect
on those. The first is the fact that we had such a short time frame at the select committee
to deal with this bill. It has been said by th e Government that that was in order to have
the legislation enacted as quickly as possible and to have it enacted before the expiry of
the temporary ban notices that were placed on some of the psychoactive products. It is
true that that is necessary. However, we did not need to  curtail the select committee
process; we simply needed to get this legislation to the House much sooner than we did.
In fact, because the Law Commission reporte d its recommendations over 2 years ago,
there has been plenty of time for the Government to make this a priority.
This is no reflection in any way whatsoev er on Peter Dunne. I know he has always
viewed this as a priority. The Government—the National Party, in particular—simply
did not prioritise this, and caused some difficulties for the select committee in dealing
with all the issues because of the shortened time frame. One of those issues was animal
testing. I do not want to dwell on that issu e too much in this speech, but suffice to say
that it was a mistake for the National Pa rty members on the committee to vote against
hearing the submissions referring to animal te sting. We needed to hear all sides of the
debate. We were not able to consider th at issue properly, because those submissions
were blocked. That was not a matter of scope; that was a question that the committee
had to make a decision on, and we did not hear those submissions, because National
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11393
Party members voted against the committee doing so. It is as si mple as that, and that is
all I really want to say about that.
We have made this bill a bett er bill. The first thing we have done is that we have
amended the purpose, and we have added th e words “to protect the health of, and
minimise harm to, individuals who use psychoactive substances.” That absolutely has to
be at the heart of this legislation. It has to be driving this legislation that its purpose is to
reduce the harm to people who use psychoactiv e substances and, indeed, to the people
around them and their communities. That is a positive change. It is incredibly positive. I
think probably the most important change for the families, the parents, and the
communities who have taken an interest in th is issue is that we have brought into the
primary legislation the banning of the sale of  psychoactive products from dairies. It will
be absolutely clear from day one, when this  legislation is passed, that it will not be
possible to buy any psychoactive product from th e local dairy. It is not appropriate for
these substances to sit alongside milk, bread, lollies, and all the other things that we buy
from our local stores. That is a massively positive change, and, in fact, I think for many
people it is the only change that is important.
There will be a transition period. There wi ll be a transition pe riod in which the
substances to which a temporary ban notice has not been applied will be able to stay on
the shelves, so long as the manufacturers of those products apply for them to become an
approved substance. To reiterate, that does not mean that there will be a transition
period in which they can continue to be sold from dairies. Again, from day one they will
be out of dairies, and that is important to note.
When the bill was originally drafted there were a number of licences available—
licences to manufacture a ps ychoactive product and licences to import a psychoactive
product. We have added in the select committee some more licences, the most important
of those being a licence to retail the product. The people who sell these products need to
be of good character, they need  to know what it is that they  are doing, they need to
know about the products, and they need to be able to provide information to the people
who are purchasing products from them. I am  very pleased that the select committee
saw fit to introduce that retailers’ licence.
We considered at length the issue of point -of-sale advertising and the packaging of
psychoactive substances. We have not gone quite  as far as plain packaging, and that is
in recognition of the fact that  not all these substances are the same. They are different
chemical compounds and they are different su bstances that have different effects on
people. But we have heavily regulated exactly  what those packages can look like. They
must not be designed in a way that appe als to young people, and they must carry
information about both the ingredients in th ose products and the pl aces that people can
seek help should they find that the product has had an adverse effect on them.
There are great restrictions on point-of -sale advertising, and, indeed, the only
advertising that will be possible will be insi de the stores that are licensed to sell these
products. My vision is that these will essent ially be stand-alone stores, into which
people will enter really only for the reason of purchasing these and associated products.
That, I think, is appropriate.  They should be R18 stores, in my view. Only people who
are 18 or over should be purchasing those products, and only people 18 and over should
be going into those stores to purchase those products.
We considered the issue of whether or not we should appl y an excise tax to these
substances. It is something that we do for alcohol and it is something that we do for
tobacco. I think it would be a positive move to apply an excise tax one day. We heard
advice from the ministry—and, indeed, the Drug Foundation supported this view—that
what we need to do is see how the market de velops and what the pricing points are, and
revisit this issue in the future when we ha ve a better idea of exactly what level of tax
11394 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
should be applied. I support that approach and I hope that we will get an opportunity to
review that in the near future.
Another issue that the select committee t ook a considerable amount of time to
consider was the issue of possession, and whet her or not it should be an offence to
possess an unapproved substance and whether or not it should be an offence for a
person aged under 18 to possess either an approved or an unapproved substance. This
was an issue that challenged the sele ct committee. Again, we gave it great
consideration, and there was c onstructive consideration from members of all parties. In
the end, the select committee came to the vi ew that for people aged under 18 making it
an offence was useful because it created th e series of events in which police could
ensure that early interven tion occurred and young people c ould be referred to health
providers—that level of early intervention would happen. The police assured us that
their first step would not be to issue an offence notice against the young person.
It is important to remember that thes e are not criminal offences; these are
infringement offences. They rate alongside a speeding fine or a parking fine, and they
do not result in a criminal record for young people. However, for the possession of an
unapproved substance by people aged 18 years or over, initially the select committee
came to the view that this was not an appr opriate thing to do, simply because it would
be so difficult for police to enforce. It is  very difficult for police to know on the spot
whether someone is in possession of an appr oved or unapproved subs tance. In fact, the
testing to determine that takes a matter of months. That does not support the notion that
this should be an on-the-spot fine. The H ealth Committee initially came to the view
that, because it did not really advance the purpose of the bill, which is to reduce the
harm relating to these psychoactive substances, it was really better to simply remove the
offence of possession of an unapproved substance.
However, the Minister came back and the G overnment insisted that we retain that
possession offence. I would lik e us to revisit that, and I have offered a Supplementary
Order Paper that we can consider during th e Committee of the whole House to revisit
that issue and possibly remove the offen ce of being in possession of an unapproved
substance. With these final words, I simply want to say that Labou r supports this bill,
and we hope that it is progressed with haste.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I am delighted to speak on the second reading of the
Psychoactive Substances Bill. I must confess that the debate this afternoon is taking
place in slightly different circumstances fr om those I had originally imagined would
occur when we talked about th is bill proceeding at this ti me. None the less, I am very
pleased with the work that the Health Committee has done in terms of its consideration
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11395
of the legislation, and with the bill that  has emerged, which looks like enjoying the

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: No, no, no.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I am sorry. I should have know n better, perhaps, than to
presume that the ACT Party would be in line with public opinion. The reason I sought
to table this petition, very simply, is that it  is indicative of the wide range of community
concern up and down New Zealand about the impact of psychoactive substances being
sold with impunity through dairies and various  other outlets by some very irresponsible
retailers. The Manurewa example was one, and I know that the member for Manurewa
and Dr Calder had been very vigorous in thei r local efforts, and I was pleased to receive
this petition.
I want to correct a myth that  has been circulatin g about this bill. It  did not actually
arise as a result of the Law Commission’s r ecommendations. In fact, the genesis of this
bill came at the UN convention on narcotic drugs meeting in Vienna in early 2011. It
became clear to me in discussions at that meeting that the British Government at that
stage was seeking to move down this path. I thought that was a particularly good idea,
and as we were developing our  interim regime, I tasked o fficials in the Ministry of
Health with finding out all we  could about what the Britis h were proposing and then
developing a regime that met our needs.  Along the way, the Law Commission made its
recommendations. The irony is that when I went back to Vienna in March this year for
the follow-up discussions, the British were  curious to know where we were, because
they were actually stalled in their efforts. In other words, we picked up their idea from 2
years ago, and had the legislatio n almost before Parliament at  that stage, and they were
still working through thei r internal bureaucracy to  get to that point and were asking us
with some envy what progress we were making and how this would occur.
I acknowledge the comments by both the Associate Minister of Health Todd McClay
and the previous speaker, Iain Lees-Gallowa y, about my own role, and I thank them for
that. It is no secret that I was frustrated with the time that it was taking to get this
legislation into the House, and I am delight ed now that we are through the process and
that the bill looks like passing fairly quickly.
This is world-breaking legislation. The r eason is it tackles the problem in quite a
lateral way. It simply says to the manufacturers and suppliers of these pernicious
substances: “You prove they are low risk, a nd if you can, we will let you sell them.” It
is a very simple proposition. Other countries—t he Australians, the Irish, the French, the
Americans, the Russians, the British, many of  the European nations  with whom I have
spoken—have all been playing the same game of trying to define what a psychoactive
substance is and how you ban it. There have been many variations on that theme. All
have come to the point of saying it is t oo difficult and asking what a way through is.
New Zealand is being looked on as world-leading in this regard. If this legislation is, as
I believe it will be, successful, then we can expect to see that model picked up and
implemented right around the world, because this issue is not one for just this country; it
is one that is affecting every jurisdicti on. When you look at the debates that are going
on in those countries and you fo llow the tenor of the argument, it is exactly the same as
we have had here over the last couple of years or so.
One of the great frustrations that I also experienced during my time as the Associate
Minister was the anger of communities who wa nted to see action, and the sense that
they had was often reflected in the comments  that I would get asking why I did not just
simply ban these things. Well, for various reasons that is not possible. Their chemical
composition is such that these things are al most indefinable. You ban one substance,
and one element is changed and the same subs tance reappears. In my time as Associate
Minister, we banned 30-odd different substa nces, over 50-odd products, and we were
11396 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
vigorous in doing so. But you can go only so far down that path. That is why this
legislation becomes vital and necessary. I make no apology for the fact that we will set a
deliberately high bar. I make no apology for the fact that th ose who want to go through
the process will pay an exorbitant fee to ge t there. There are huge proceeds involved
from this trade, and I think it is only fair and reasonable to expose those people to a very
rigorous standard of testing a nd a very rigorous process befo re we even get to the point
where they get on to the market.
Let me deal with one of the great red herrings of this debate, the animal testing issue.
There was never any intention—ever—to embark upon a programme of animal testing
associated with these products. There was never ever any intent. What happened was
simply this. What happened—

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: There was going to be.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: If the member would just give me the courtesy of some
silence, I will explain to him what actually happened. Late last year an Official
Information Act request was lodged with the Ministry of Health for a whole range of
papers relating to this new regime. One of the papers was a paper prepared by Dr Leo
Schep of the National Poisons Centre in D unedin. Dr Schep has done a huge amount of
work in this area, but is at one end of the spectrum in terms of the debate. He is a purist.
I acknowledge that. He is an exceptional toxico logist, but he is a purist. He produced a
paper that was headed “Report to the New Zealand Government on Animal Testing”. It
was his initiative. Unfortunately, when we s ought to release that batch of papers I did
not check the title page. What appeared in the Sunday Star-Times was: “Here is an
official report to the New Zealand Government recommending animal testing.” It was
an unsolicited piece of advice. That was why I ruled out—very immediately—the LD50
test. That was why I worked with the se lect committee through th e expert advisory
committee to make sure that the instances where animal testing might be even a
possibility were minimised and reduced. But I say to the House it was never the
intention—

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Is there any animal testing? Is there any animal testing?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Mr Banks, if you ask a question, it is customary to let the
person answer it before you come back with the next one.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: OK. Will there be any animal testing?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I am just in the process of explaining to the yabbering
preacher to my left the answer to his question. It was never the intention to embark upon
an animal testing regime as part of this legislation.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Will there be animal testing?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Can I explain again. This is becoming like a routine. It was
never the intention to  embark upon any form of animal  testing. The expert advisory
committee has given very clear advice to the se lect committee. The reality is that a lot
of the stuff—and I am still getting emails today in Cyrillic script, in various different
languages, from around the world from pe ople saying: “Don’t test psychoactive
substances on dogs.” That was never the intention.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Will it happen?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: It was never going to happen. The member says: “Will it
happen?”. Can I say it was never going to happen.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Will it happen?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Dear me. You can go only so far in terms of legislating—

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Will it happen: yes or no? Will animal testing—

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Can I say again to the member: it was never the intention.
How many words does he need to explain it? I am not going—

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: No, you won’t, you puppy-hater.
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11397

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Oh, that is absolute, ridicul ous nonsense. If the member for
Epsom wants to go out there and oppose this  legislation, he ca n answer to his
communities, he can answer to the parents and to all of the people affected by it, and he
will be the one who will be reviled as the person out of step with public opinion. I say to
the ACT Party that if it wants to show a ny form of relevance,  it will grow up, it will
respect the conscience of Ne w Zealanders on this issue,  and it will support this
legislation. He is welcome to be out on a limb; it will be a very lonely place, I assure
him.
The bulk of New Zealanders want to see this  legislation passed immediately. It will
be, and I acknowledge the support of the Government. I acknowledge the support of
other parties that take an appro ach in this particular legislation that is beneficial. This is
the opportunity to make huge progress. The world is watching us. I think this
Parliament will not only do the people of  New Zealand and the young people of New
Zealand a huge service in passi ng this legislation but will set a standard that other
nations will follow. Hopefully, working collec tively at an international level, we can
start to turn back the clock on this particular issue.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on the
Psychoactive Substances Bill in this second reading. I am also a very proud member of
the Health Committee, which, as my colleague Iain Lees-Galloway has said, has worked
very, very collaboratively to bring to the Hous e a piece of legislation that I think we are
all very proud of. I want to acknowledge the Hon Peter Dunne and the leadership that he
has shown in bringing this pi ece of legislation to the Hous e, and to also thank him for
tabling a petition on beha lf of 3,533 members of th e Manurewa community. In
acknowledging that petition being tabled, I want to acknowledge Jan Lim, who owns a
chemist’s on Great South Road, very near  a legal high shop that was established 2
months ago, I believe to dump these products  as this legislation progressed through the
House. In acknowledging Jan, I want to acknowledge Dr Tim Wilkinson, who owns and
manages the health centre next  door to this legal high s hop, and who has worked very
hard to be a representative and an advocat e of our community. I want to acknowledge
Mr Youkhanis, who is the barber in the store next to the le gal high shop in my
Manurewa electorate, and also young people such as Meliana Ngata, who is the chair of
the Manurewa Youth Council,  and Warriors of Change representatives Benjamin
Tamarua and Susan Fotunga, who organised a march for the community of Manurewa
to come out against this legal high shop but  in support of the Psychoactive Substances
Bill.
The main point that I want to make in my contribution, really, is about the select
committee process and the number of changes or  amendments to the original legislation
that we have worked so collaboratively on. I would like to highlight, for example, that
in the original purpose statement for this particular bill, nowhere did we state that this
bill was about protecting the health of, and minimising the harm to, individuals who use
psychoactive substances. The committee came to the conclusion that, actually, this was
about instituting a regulatory regime, but, coup led with that, the hear t of this legislation
was to make sure that New Zealanders in the consumption of these products were going
to be safe. That, I think, is a very fundame ntal point about this piece of legislation,
because these substances are not drugs. These substances are not foods. These
substances were pretty much unregulated. They were nothings that a whole lot of people
capitalised on, packaged up, and sold to New Zealanders. The reality of these
substances was that they were hurting our community. Technically, I think, they were
poisons. So the ability of the select committee,  yes, to institute a regulatory regime, but
fundamentally to say that at the heart of this legislation we are going to protect the
health and safety of New Zealanders is something that needs to be acknowledged.
11398 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
I certainly received, and I know that many of the Health Committee members
received, communications, part icularly from mental health workers who were very
concerned about their ability to engage constructively, particularly with young people
who were going through counselling because th ey had addictions. The fact was that
these substances were legal substances, so they may have got off the drugs, but they
were getting into these psychoactive substanc es. And also one of the things that we
made very clear was that there could be a de mand on public services in terms of mental
health and addiction services. We particul arly wanted to highl ight that that was
something that the select committee had obvi ously heard and was concerned about. So
we have given notice to the he alth Minister and to the health sector that that is a
possible consequence of this bill going th rough and regulation of these particular
products.
I also want to highlight a couple of othe r substantive debates that we had. One of
them was around the age of purchase. It wa s very interesting b ecause, again, all the
professionals who understand addiction and who understand the development of our
brains are particularly concer ned about how these substances  engage or interact with
young people’s consumption. Again,  we are all very clear th at we should actually have
an age of purchase of either 20 or 21. It di d, I guess, inspire a lot of heated discussion
around the table within the cont ext of a bill that we had approved just recently as a
Parliament in terms of the alcohol consum ption age. Fundamentally, I think what we
have done is reinforce a decision that this Parliament had previously made. I have to say
that I stood on the side of making the age of purchase either 20 or 21, based on the
scientific evidence.
At the end of the day, as you will see and as people will s ee if they read  this bill,
what we have primarily done is said that these psychoactive substances fit into the
category of either alcohol or tobacco, whic h is what a lot of the initiatives or
amendments to this legislation have replic ated. In doing that, we then had to be
consistent. We could not say that psychoact ive substances were worse and so they
deserved a higher age of consumption, becau se from our perspective alcohol, tobacco,
and psychoactive substances —all of these products—have detrimental effects,
particularly on young people. So to the Manurewa Youth Council and to the young
people of Manurewa, who were very clear to both me and Cam Calder that we should
be advocating for an increase in the age of purchase, that is the rationale. Hopefully,
they will understand that that is the position that we came to.
The other heated discussion we had was a bout whether or not we  should provide a
mechanism for the police to engage with  young people under the age of 18 who are in
possession of a substance, whether it be  an approved substa nce or an unapproved
substance. What we did in the end was to  enable the police—through them coming to
the Health Committee—to be empowered to  engage with young pe ople and, basically,
to confiscate any psychoactive substance that they have in  their possession. To enable
them to do that, we had to create an offen ce, but we as a select committee were very
clear that it would not be a criminal o ffence. We do not want young people to be
criminalised for being in po ssession of psychoactive substa nces. But what we did want
was for the police to have the tool to enga ge with young people. It was our hope that in
engaging, they would actually look at whether or  not health or social services were an
appropriate medium. At wors t-case scenario, there would be an infringement for
possession, but it will not be a criminal offence.
I would like just briefly to  touch on the aspects of spons orship and advertising. The
select committee was very clear that any retailer or manufacturer of psychoactive
substances would not be able to advertis e the product or provide sponsorship of the
product that then puts the product out into the market. Advertisi ng, particularly, is
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11399
relevant to the shop in the heart of our Ma nurewa community, the High Zone shop, so
we were very clear and we insisted on a specific provision, clause 53A, which sets out
restrictions on what retailers can call shops . From our perspectiv e, that has been
specifically put in to ensure that High Zone  shops or legal high shops cannot advertise
and establish themselves in communities like ours. The other thing that we were very
clear about was that local people—our lo cal boards—have to be involved in the
decision making about where these shops are established. We made specific mention of
these shops not being near schools, not being able to have a detrimental effect on young
people particularly. What I say to Angela Dalton, who is  the chair of the Manurewa
Local Board, to Colleen Brown, to Simeon Brown, and to Toa Greening, who all made
submissions on this bill, is that this piece of  legislation will give you the tools so that
you can protect our communities.
I want to thank once again my fellow committee members. It was a very constructive
process. I look forward to this bill being pa ssed as soon as possible, because we have to
get these products off the shelves and out of our communities. I commend the bill to the
House. Thank you.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Could I begin, as others have done, by congratulating
and thanking other members of the Health  Committee who considered the Psychoactive
Substances Bill. I believe that we collec tively did a pretty good job. As Iain Lees-
Galloway has said, we worked very collegial ly, apart from, I think, on one issue, which
I will come to later on. I also want to thank the officials from the Ministry of Health and
other departments who worked with us on this  bill. We were given a tight time frame to
work in, and they worked very well under pressure.
In the first reading debate I praised the bill  for a variety of things. It is world-first
legislation. It provides a framework that bases our response to these substances on
health effects. It is a framework that ma kes the regulatory response proportional to the
harm that is being prevented. It  is a framework that sets the bar at low risk, not no risk.
So it is not a prohibition-base d response to these substances , which, I think, is practical
and visionary recognition of what works a nd what does not work in regulating such
substances.
We are a country that has been very much at the forefront of this debate. We were
pretty much the first country to experience  the wave of psychoact ive substances, with
the benzylpiperazine products. We were the first country to go into the failed regime of
temporary prohibition notices. Now here we are, the first count ry to be developing this
kind of framework, which is modern, proportionate, and rational drug policy.
Accordingly, the review that we do of this legislation in 5 years’ time—and I am very
pleased that the Government has built that in to the bill—is going to be very important.
It is going to enable us to learn from it and it is going to enable the rest of the world to
learn from it too.
In my first reading speech I indicated a number of areas that needed improvement. I
want to run through those very quickly. Othe rs have touched on some of them. I said
that improving health had to be clearly st ated in the purpose of the bill. Improving
health and reducing harm are now very clearly stated, as others have pointed out. I said
that the bill needed to define  what low risk constituted. Th e bill does not do that. I have
to say—and this is, I guess, the strength  of our select committee process in New
Zealand—that I changed my mind. Submitters  to the bill changed my mind on that
issue, and I agree that actually it is better fo r practice to inform that definition, and that
is what is going to happen.
I indicated that a number of the measures th at are used in the c ontrol of alcohol and
tobacco ought to be brought over and used in this bill also, to add to the suite of tools
available for regulation of psychoactive subs tances. We looked at controls of location,
11400 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
hours, sponsorship, advertising, labelling, and price in relation to each of those
substances—alcohol and tobacco—and on most of those fronts we have now added in
the possibility to regulate those matters.
Iain Lees-Galloway has mentioned the reasons that we have not moved on excise tax
at this time. Like Mr Lees-Galloway, I also was convinced by submitters on that point. I
was initially a fan of plain packaging, and I changed my mind about that too. I changed
my mind on the basis that, unlike tobacco, the psychoactive substances that we are
dealing with are not all ones th at uniformly cause harm. In fact, the ones that we are
allowing through the gate with this bill are ones that, by definition, carry low risk, so the
same level of response that we have on tobacco is not appropriate. Also, these
substances are not all the same. Unlike a ciga rette or a pouch of tobacco, which is more
or less the same thing regardless of who th e manufacturer is, these substances are
actually different; they do different things. So plain packaging is not appropriate.
In my first reading speech I called for a shorter transition peri od, and that has been
adopted. I also called for the licensing of reta ilers, and that has also been adopted. I
think that is a very good development. Overall, what we see with this bill is, I think, the
beginning of a convergence of the way that we  approach the regulation of substances
that cause harm, but, none the less, as a soci ety we say that a pers on ought to have the
right to use that substance a nd to engage with that harm. I think that convergence is a
very good thing, and certainly one of the things that I look forward to  in the future is
further convergence of the regulation of these kinds of substances.
Back in the first reading speech I expresse d the hope that we would offer the world a
model that would be worthy of being worl d-leading. I think that, with a couple of
exceptions, we have done that. I just want to come to those exceptions now. One is
around the possession offences. There has already been some discussion here today. The
bill contains an infringement offence for possessing an unapproved substance. I think
that that should be scrapped, and I really  hope that the Minister —and I appreciated his
words today—will consider doing that, an d that the House does in fact have
opportunities to do so.
The result of possession offences in the Misuse of Drugs Act has not been to see
more people treated, it has not been to see less consumption, and it has not been to see
less harm, and there is no reason to suppose th at any of those woul d be the effect of
including a possession offence here. Instead, what it mainly has done is it has tied up
police time and punished people. I do not know th at that is really consistent with the
objective that we now have for this bill. Ther e have not been possession offences in the
temporary prohibition notices, and not a singl e person has been clamouring for there to
be such possession offences. So the non-exis tence of such offen ces under those notices
has not been a problem, and if there is no t a problem, we do not need to provide a
solution for it.
As Mr Lees-Galloway has mentioned, the idea of infringement notices is to provide
an on-the-spot response to a minor offence. In fact, in this case an  on-the-spot response
is not possible, because the testing to determine whether this is an approved or
unapproved substance takes months. So it is out of kilter with infringement notices—the
rubric upon which those are ba sed—it provides no real benef it, and there is significant
harm. I do not believe, on balance, that it is worthwhile. The minority report refers to
the under-18s issue, and we ar e going to be watching that  closely, because we believe
that that is likely to be used more to ha rass young people than to actually result in their
receiving treatment.
The other issue that I address in the mi nority report—and it has to be addressed, I
believe, by this House; and my colleague Mojo Mathers will speak more about it—is
the animal testing issue. The fact is that the previous Associate Minister of Health
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11401
encouraged people to make submissions about animal testing. The committee did
receive advice from the Clerk of the House that amendments that absolutely ruled out
animal testing per se would be out of scope. We received no advice that those
submissions were out of scope. So the chair was wrong to rule those submissions out of
scope. The National majority was wrong to not hear those submissions.
How it stands now is that a whole bunch of New Zealande rs have been effectively
disenfranchised from their opportunity to ha ve a say about this bill. The only people
now to have actually read those submissions —and we provide a littl e bit of flavour in
the minority report, demonstrating how there are suitable alternatives to animal testing
to establish safety—are the Green Party memb ers, because we held our own hearings to
hear those submissions.
That is not how the process ought to work. It is not how the process ought to work.
We must adopt Mojo Mathers’ Supplementary Order Paper 260 in the Committee stage,
in order to have that world-best practice— that model for the rest of the world. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I rise to oppose the Psychoactive Substances
Bill, and I will oppose it at ever y turn until it ends up on the statute book with the
numbers, except for me, in this House. This bill is well intentione d—there is no doubt
about that—and is aimed at ensuring that ps ychoactive substances sold in New Zealand
are as safe as possible. I want to pay my  respects to the new A ssociate Minister of
Health, Todd McClay, for his noble intentions with this bill, which he inherited from the
ex - Associate Minister. However, I simply cannot support it.
I find it totally unacceptable that this bill fails to rule out—to rule out—testing these
recreational drugs on innocent animals. Protec ting animals is ingrained in my soul. I
think most New Zealanders will be outraged at the idea that chemicals people use just
for fun can be, and likely will be, tested on harmless animals. Animals will be put to
extreme pain, animals will suffer, and animals will die. That is why the countries in the
European Union have banned the testing of cosmetics on animals—in particular,
rabbits.
We must remember that psychoactive drug substances are not a necessity, and we
should say to people today, from this Parlia ment, that they are high-risk substances
under any circumstances—they are not a n ecessity for the well-being of the human
person. Recreational drugs are not something one needs to consume. They are not
something people should consume. We should say, from this Parliament today, that
young people, any person, should not be consum ing these substances. That is the first
message. They are not lifesaving medicines or  something that will relieve suffering.
People do not need to take these chemicals.
Their prolific use will cause widespread  animal suffering. There is simply no
justification or reason for unnecessary drugs like these to be tested on animals, and I for
one find it deeply offensive that any Gove rnment would sanction this. Animals will be
in pain and animals will die in the name of people wanting to take mind-altering drugs
on the weekend. That is simply wrong and una cceptable. Animals must not experience
suffering for economic or entertainment reasons , or for lining the pockets of the drug
importers and the drug dealers who will be selling them at the dairies to addle the minds
of our kids.
I know the Health Committee inserted a new cl ause in the bill to state that animal
testing should be used only when necessary. But animal testing will  never be necessary
for recreational drug purposes. It will never be  necessary to cruelly treat a beagle puppy
in the name of a recreational party drug. Evidence shows animal testing is not necessary
at all to prove the safety of these mind- altering chemicals. Dr Ian Shaw of the
University of Canterbury says that non-animal  testing can adequately establish whether
11402 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
a substance has an unacceptable risk of acute toxicity. Cell culture, ex vivo, and
structure-activity relationship studies can all be used to establish the risk. Non-animal
testing regimes can test all of these substances to establish the risk.
I cannot for the life of me see the misc hief in allowing the good people of Save
Animals from Exploitation and the SPCA to come to the select committee to make a
submission. What would have been the mischi ef of saying to these good Samaritans in
our community who protect harmless animals from cruelty: “Come to the select
committee of the Parliament and have your say.”? I know why they were not allowed. It
was because the ex - Associate Minister of  Health would have been embarrassed by
what they would have had to say about our ob ligations to treat animals with respect and
dignity.
This afternoon in the House the ex - Associ ate Minister said: “It’s not our intention
to test these substances on animals.” He said  it four times: “It’s not our intention.” I
interjected from that seat there: “Tell me, ex-Minister, will animals be used for
testing?”. He said: “It’s not our intenti on.” The road to hell is paved with good
intentions. I asked the ex-Minister four times. The naive ex-Minister said “It’s not our
intention. It’s never been our intention.”, but that is not what the bill says. The bill does
not rule out the testing on beagle puppies of these mind-altering, dangerous chemicals.
It does not rule it out.
There would be no mischief whatsoever in taking Mojo Mathers’ Supplementary
Order Paper 260 and embracing it, and then we would have worl d-class, leading
legislation on mind-altering s ubstances that will be sold  by the drug dealers and the
dairies on the corner, mainly to our young pe ople. We would have that there. What
would have been the mischief ? What would have been th e mischief of taking Mojo
Mathers’ Supplementary Order Paper? It wa s a pigheaded attitude by the ex-Minister
that stopped it, and nothing more. I know my friends in the National Party on the select
committee would not have worried if that had been the directive from the ex-Minister.
But the ex-Minister could not see it in his heart and in his soul to protect harmless
animals from being treated with these dangerous drugs.
If you cannot prove your fun dr ug of choice is safe without  putting animals in abject
misery, you cannot sell the drug. If you need to pay more for more expensive, non-
animal testing in China, where it will be tested, I say tough luck, again. That is the price
you pay, and that is the price you have to pay for the profiteers of these dangerous
chemicals who sell them to our kids. The real ity is the bill could well result in drugs
being tested on animals in places like China and India, where animal welfare is
shamefully non-existent. Most of these substanc es will be tested in China and in India,
where there are no animal welfare rights, no animal welfare care, and no responsibility.
The statement in the bill that overseas test ing must be carried out in accordance with
the New Zealand Animal Welfare Act is nonsen se because there is no way for us in
New Zealand to assess what goes on in the torture chambers of animal testing
laboratories in South-east Asia . There is no way we can test  there. There is no way we
can put our high standards of animal welfare on regimes there. Despite assurances from
the ex-Minister, this bill fails to rule out the use of extremely cruel LD50 tests. We will
wait and see where that goes, and we will talk about it later.
But, even worse, these animal testing places test their drugs on man’s best friends, as
I said—dogs, or, more important, on beagle puppies bred for purpose. Some have said
that Mr Kerridge, the eminent Mr Kerridge  from the SPCA, supports this. Nothing
could be further from the truth. Mr Kerridge ha s told me: “It is a matter of record that I
am opposed to any animal testing for the approval of psychoactive products, and my
presence on this committee does not alter or condone it at all.”
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11403
Finally, I want to thank Mojo Mather s for her work on this bill and her
Supplementary Order Paper, which I will be supporting. I am sure other parties will
support it as well. But I say to  her and the Green Party that  if your amendment fails at
the Committee stage to get th e numbers, you should vote agai nst this bill anyway. The
Green Party has an excellent set of credenti als around animal rights and animal welfare,
and I applaud it today for those.
We are sacrificing animals at the altar of recreational drug-use. It is a disgrace to this
country. It should not happen. It does not need  to happen. We could stop it. It could be
world-leading education. I repeat these words: as the most powerful creatures on this
earth, humans have a responsibility to protect all animals from senseless, worthless, and
shameless cruelty at all times and in all places, and I am starting with this legislation
here today in this Parliament.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I stand on behalf of New Zealand First to
support the Psychoactive Substances Bill. Th is bill has been a long time coming. It has
taken a long time for the former Associate Minister of Health to front up to the
problems caused by legal highs, but we have th is legislation here now and we now find
that we could be world leaders in this area. I would also like to acknowledge the chair of
the Health Committee, Dr Paul Hutchison.  He has done a wonderf ul job with this
legislation, particularly when one takes into account the views that many of us had prior
to going to the select committee. Thank you too to the rest of the select committee. It
was a very constructive process, helped out by the committee officials.
Ideally—and before we went to the se lect committee—New Zealand First would
have liked to see these substances banned. We know they are a very high risk, but
during the select committee process we ha d our opinions changed, because these
products contain many ingredients that ar e commonly available for purchase now. Of
course, the former Associate Minister, th e Hon Peter Dunne, outlined at quite some
length the reasons as to why these products could not be banned. But the bottom line is
that New Zealand First did not want our young people going for a trip, never leaving the
building, never leaving the street, and coming back with massive challenges as baggage.
Week in, week out, we have seen reports of these substances leading our young people
into crime and reports of the serious harm that is being created by the consumption of
these untested products. The bottom line is that  we still do not know what the long-term
effects are of consumption of these products.
We know that petty offences are taking pl ace and, of course, serious crimes. The
effects that these substances have on one’s well-being have been widely documented. It
has been shameful that under the current le gislation New Zealanders have had very
limited means to actually prevent harmful subs tances from being sold, manufactured, or
even imported into New Zealand. We have  been putting the manufacturers of these
substances ahead of the well-being of everyday New Zealanders. These companies have
been able to manufacture new legal highs. They import them and distribute them as they
please. The Government has been always behind the eight ball,  having to try to
continually monitor these dr ugs, and placing every dodgy s ubstance on the misuse of
drugs register when it became a problem. Consequently, the Government was always
left two steps behind, running to try to catch  up, and that is not a good situation when
the Government is actually supposed to be running the country.
New Zealand First supports this bill because it actually protects the health and safety
of New Zealanders, which is most importa nt. We know that legal highs are largely
detrimental to our nation’s health. Unfortunately, they are lucrative to the manufacturers
and the sellers. Most of the time we do not know what is in these substances or the
effects that they are going to have on people.  We are going to have a change on this
front, which is very positive.
11404 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
Legal highs are basically being marketed blind, without the purchaser knowing, or
even caring about, what they contain and how they can encourage dangerous behaviour,
and without them knowing that legal highs may make people seriously ill, that they
should not be used in association with alc ohol, and that they can  even endanger young
lives. We constantly read pages and pages of news in various newspapers, right
throughout the country, of how Ne w Zealanders have put them selves at risk by taking
these legal highs. We know that these substa nces are associated with numerous mental
health issues, violence—a whol e range of issues. So they are not good products as they
currently stand.
The purchasing and the advertis ing restrictions are adequa te for the time being. Like
previous speakers, we initially thought that these products should have been restricted to
those who are over 20. We have got a very co nservative view on the age of purchase,
but we have agreed that perhaps the legislation should be in line with the alcohol
legislation. The ban on sales from dairies and having no advertising at point of sale is
also good. We needed to have something in this way. It is not good enough when bags
of sweets are given away by dairy owners, who did not really want these products
associated with drug dealing. It is a bad situ ation when we are allowing dairy owners to
be the legalised drug dealers in the comm unity. These products should not be sold
alongside newspapers and chocolate and iceblocks and sweets, but  this bill will sort out
this problem, which we are very happy about.
I was talking to my taxi driver, and he had actually been sent into a dairy to purchase
one of these products, along with a can of V, for the woman who required it. He was
actually looking in the freezer part of the cabinet. He thought  that it was perhaps some
sort of iceblock, or perhap s another product like V. He wa s shocked to find out that it
was actually synthetic cannabis that he was carrying in his taxi to take back to the
customer.
New Zealand First supports the provisions in the bill that wish to make
manufacturers prove that their products are safe. The testing should be the responsibility
of the manufacturer. They make mega-money from  this particular product, so it is time
they ensured that their products are legitim ate and that the substances they contain
provide only a low risk for consumers. The onus has to be on the manufacturers here.
New Zealand First, along with others, want ed plain packaging for these particular
products, but throughout the select committee pr ocess we, like other parties, changed
our mind on this particular as pect. We are very happy with  the labelling requirements
that are going to require all products to ha ve their active ingred ients listed, a phone
number for the National Poisons Centre, the contact details for the product’s New
Zealand manufacturer or supplier, plus a warn ing that it should not be consumed with
alcohol.
The bill is a much-needed start at regulating the uses of psychoactive substances; it is
something that we are very pleased to see. One of the issues that we believe should be at
the forefront for all New Zealanders is the health and safety of our young people,
particularly when we read in the paper a bout the growing violence  that is created by
these substances. Psychoactive substances need  to be heavily regulated. We have got
paramedics speaking out about how these le gal highs are now a much larger problem
than the illicit drugs that are available.
New Zealand First supports the tough new pe nalties that this bill will actually
introduce: 8 years in prison for importing, ma king, or supplying banned substances, and
2 years in prison for importing, making, or supplying untested substances. We believe
that this bill is a very positive step forw ard. These drugs will be tried and tested. We
will not have these drugs in dairies, and we know that advertising is not going to be as
widespread as it is at this point. It is fo r all of these reasons that New Zealand First
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11405
supports this bill and we look forward to its speedy passage through the House. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak on this very innovative Psychoactiv e Substances Bill. I would like to
acknowledge and thank, first of  all, the Hon Peter Dunne, who has pressed on with this
bill. I was under the impression that the bi ll came about through the Law Commission’s
recommendations, but he has told us this afternoon that it was through a United Nations
committee. I think the main point is that this  bill requires manuf acturers to show that
these substances are of minimal risk. Might  I also acknowledge a nd thank the officials
and the Health Committee, which has generally worked extremely well to achieve a
very good result.
Finally, might I thank and acknowledge the submitters. There were powerful
submissions from right around New Zealand. I remember specifically the Mayor of
Timaru coming up and saying that in her co mmunity this was the No. 1 problem and
that there were four or fi ve shops, dairies, selling th ese substances to young people.
They even texted young people when a new high came in, and they would come to the
back door and sell them.
From Manurewa we had three submissions. People were absolutely outraged by the
way that High Zone was carrying on business in that community, next to a doctor’s
surgery and next to a shopping centre wher e lots of young people went. Since those
submissions I have been rung up by them, to be  told that they have just heard that a
truckload or planeloads of subs tances that have come from Pakistan have landed in the
wharves and at the airport in  Auckland, and they are basica lly loading up prior to the
date that this bill is enacted. I think that  is a great worry, and it is a warning to our
officials to make sure that they rigorously pursue the regulations associated with this
bill. Certainly I would like to acknowledge Cam Calder for all the work that he has
done, along with Louisa Wall, in supporting the Manurewa community and, of course,
the individuals who have been devastated  by their children being involved with
cannabinoids and various other legal highs.
In my own community, Waiuku, the supermar ket owners have set up a campaign to
reduce these substances, and three of the four  dairies have already spontaneously said:
“No, we’re not going to have anything to do with them.”, and I think that is very good.
I would like to comment on the basic purpose of the bill, which indeed is to regulate
the availability of psychoactive substances. It  was one of the amendments of the select
committee—and it was supported by submissions—t o include: “to protect the health of,
and minimise harm to, individuals who use psychoactive substances.” I think that was
very much in line with the al cohol legislation and with othe r such legislation that we
have in New Zealand, and I applaud that.
The expert advisory committee has some ma jor tasks ahead, and its working will be
pivotal to this bill. The committee, of cour se, has to advise the authority. Its experts
include those in pharmacology, toxicology, neur oscience, medicine, and several others.
On this occasion it has included Bob Kerridge, and he has been absolutely clear about
his opposition to animal testing, and I acknowledge that.
The offences in this bill are very cl ear. For manufacturers th ey are high—up to 2
years’ jail and $500,000. We had considerable debate about sanctions for possession for
those under 18 and those over 18. Undoubtedly, we  also had advice from the police,
who were clear in what they wanted. I think we have come out with a good steer in this
bill that infringement notices are there but that they will not be criminal, particularly for
young people. The police know well that they want to ensure that rehabilitation is the
way to go, rather than down the criminal track.
11406 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013
I also want to just make note of the fact that, indeed, many places will have
restrictions on sales, not only shops, grocery stores, supe rmarkets, and garages, but, in
fact, any other place or premise specified or  described in the regulations. Already, I
understand, there has been a suggestion that vi deo stores may try to sell these things.
More important was the select committee putting in clause 61A, which relates that a
territorial authority may have a policy relating to the sale  of approved products within
its districts, which is similar to the alcohol legislation. I think that is very useful and will
be welcomed in Manurewa.
Finally, I come to animal testing. Firstly, I want to just comment on the advice from
the Clerk of the House, because it was very clear initially on 26 April 2013. Then later,
on 5 June, the Clerk of the House confir med the initial advice that amendments
prohibiting testing psychoactive substances  on animals were beyond the scope of the
bill, as the bill is about approval and licensi ng of the substances, and not their testing.
On 5 June the Office of the Clerk said it could advise that an amendment to preclude the
use of information derived from animal te sting of psychoactive substance products in
support of any application for approval may be in order—may be in order.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: So all the submissions would have been relevant.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I absolutely reject what Kevin Hague has said regarding
the process, and will not resile from the position that we took on the advice from the
Clerk of the House.
Secondly, I come to the advice of the expe rt advisory committee. It came to its
recommendations through a consensus process. It decided to come to “a consensus
position … followed by a majority and minority report if consensus was not possible.”
No minority report was needed, and it was on the recommendations of the expert
advisory committee that we came to an am endment that satisfied, ostensibly, all
members of the select committee: “The a dvisory committee must ensure that any
preclinical or clinical test s … that relate to a psycho active product do no t rely on any
research, testing, or teaching that involves the use of an animal if suitable alternatives
exist.” What is absolutely clear is what  the expert advisory committee then came up
with, because it said this: “The Committee cons iders that it is not currently possible to
completely prohibit animal testing and some animal testing may be necessary to provide
data to support human research in order to allow the legislation to deliver its primary
aim. The Committee recommends that some anim al testing be permitted.” I think that is
very, very important to underscore.

items.speaker: The final point is this
items.text: having looked very ca refully at the intern ational best-practice
scientific community, there is  no question but that animal  testing—though it should be
minimised—is necessary. Undoubtedly, rigorous  testing is required to demonstrate
minimal risk, particularly when tens of thousands of users are young adults and
adolescents. I very much hope that the La bour Party—given that it s current leader, Mr
Shearer, is also its scien ce spokesman—will support an evidence-based approach and
support his health team. Not to do so, I believe, would be utterly irresponsible.
Just to end, there is no question but that the major purpose of this bill is excellent. It
is to regulate psychoactive substances and to  protect the health of, and minimise harm
to, individuals who use them in this country. Thank you.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: I welcome the opportunity to
speak at the second reading of this bill, th e Psychoactive Substances Bill. It is an
important opportunity to talk about the absolute hope that is  out there in the
communities throughout New Zealand that this  bill is going through the House as
quickly as possible, and that it will go some way to addressing some of the terrible harm
that is being done in our community by the ps ychoactive substances that are prevalent.
First of all, I would like to just put on th e record—if it has not b een put on the record
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11407
already—my congratulations to our spokesper son on this bill, Iain Lees-Galloway, who
has done such a great job on pushing this forw ard. It was he who sa id very loudly last
year that this change should be happening and should have happened sooner. In fact, he
said that we think it is ridiculous that we have basically been experimenting on our kids
by allowing the substances to come on the shelf, and then constantly chasing our tails
trying to get them off the shel f again. That absolutely encapsulates just what has been
happening in communities throughout New Zealand. Although I certainly do also
acknowledge my colleague Louisa Wall, who has been working extremely hard in her
community in Manurewa, there are many othe r communities for which this is a terrible
scourge and in which there are terrible harms being done.
I want to talk in my speech on this bill about some of the harm that has been done in
my community in Dunedin, but before I do that I would also like to just point out that it
must be said that this Government has not taken the opportunity to completely overhaul
the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. In 1975 many of  the people who are standing in this
House were not even born. Many things have actually moved on since then.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Not all of the members of th e House—some of them were
probably sitting in this House in 1975, but onl y a very few. But certainly times have
changed, and, as we know, the composition of drugs has changed, the way that they are
being taken has changed, and our ability to re spond to drug abuse has changed. The
only thing that has not changed is the law.
I just want to say what ha s actually brought me to be sp eaking about this particular
issue today. It was th e community that came into my of fice earlier this year and raised
this with me. There was a stream of pe ople from the community talking about the
absolute importance of making change ha ppen and making change quickly, and the
impact that this problem has had on so  many young people in the community. For
example, there was the woman who came into  my office to offer me her support and
give me her story on how she had been affected by taking these drugs. She had just
come out of a psychiatric institution.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 6 p.m.

27 Jun 2013 Business Statement 11355 
THURSDAY, 27 JUNE 2013 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN (Minister of Defence) on behalf of the Leader 
of the House : When the House resumes on Tuesday, 2 July the Government will look 
to make progress on the State Sector and Public Finance Reform Bill, the Psychoactive 
Substances Bill, and the Appropriation ( 2013/14 Estimates) Bill. Wednesday is a 
members’ day. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economic Programme—Progress  
1. MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore)  to the Minister of Finance : How 
has the Government’s economic plan helped New Zealand families to get ahead since 
the recession five years ago? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Actin g Minister of Finance) : I can confirm that the 
Government’s economic plan is helping families in many ways. The Government has 
clearly set out a strong plan for the economy. We  have stuck to that plan and we have 
taken New Zealanders with us, as the latest polls confirm. The plan is about responsibly 
managing the Government’s finances so that New Zealanders’ taxes are spent wisely on 
the services that they need. It is about building a more competitive and productive 
economy to create more jobs, raise income s, and build opportunities here in New 
Zealand. It is about deliveri ng better public services for families, such as schools, 
hospitals, and keeping communities safe, and it is about rebuilding Christchurch so that 
Canterbury families can get their lives back on track. 
Maggie Barry : What are some of the signs of  progress with the Government’s 
economic programme? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : There are several positive i ndicators. Firstly, the economy 
grew by 2.4 percent in the 12 months to 31 March. This is better than most developed 
countries. Secondly, there are around 50,000 more  jobs in the economy than there were 
2 years ago. Thirdly, the cost of living is increasing by less than 1 percent—its lowest 
rate in more than 13 years. Fourthly, the unemployment levels have been the lowest 
they have been since the global financial crisis, but, of course, there is still more work to 
do there. The Government is on track to surplus in 2014-15, so that we can start 
repaying debt on behalf of New Zealanders. All of these things are very positive for 
New Zealand families. 
Maggie Barry: What do the latest official statistics show about growth in wages? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The quarterly employment survey from Statistics New 
Zealand shows that average full-time weekly wages, including overtime, rose 2.6 
percent over the last year. This compares wi th inflation over the la st year of only 0.9 
percent. Over the last 2 years the aver age wage, including overtime, has risen 6.1 
percent, and that compares with 2.4 percen t inflation over those 2 years. Of course, 
every individual has their own particular circumstances, but it is quite clear that on 
average wages have been rising considerably fa ster than the cost of  living, which is an 
important indicator that families are getting ahead. 
Maggie Barry: How have wages in the manufacturing sector performed in the past 
year, and how does that compare with the situation in 2008? 
11356 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Jun 2013 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The average wage in the ma nufacturing sector, including 
overtime, increased 5.2 percent, or, in other words, twice as fast as wages in the 
economy as a whole. In fact, since the be ginning of 2009, the average wage in the 
manufacturing sector has rise n a total of 18 percent, ma king it the second-strongest 
sector of the economy in terms of wage grow th. That strong wage growth is in marked

to dispose of an average jury trial. They will also remove more than 30,000 unnecessary
