the end of 2013. The bill paves the way for a new set of mining regulations that will 
improve health and safety in the mining industry and bring New Zealand’s regulation of 
11374 Health and Safety (Pike Rive r Implementation) Bill 27 Jun 2013 
mining health and safety in line with intern ational best practice. We owe this to the 
workers who lost their lives at Pike River, and to their families, and to all current and 
future workers in the mining industry.  
The bill before us today is an omnibus b ill. It addresses those recommendations of 
the royal commission that require new or amende d primary legislation. It will establish 
a new stand-alone Crown agent, WorkSafe New Zealand, to focus on workplace health 
and safety, it will amend the Health and Safe ty in Employment Act, and it will replace 
the Mines Rescue Trust Act.  
The first part of this bill, as I have said, establishes WorkSafe New Zealand. The 
creation of a stand-alone Crown agent with a dedicated focus on health and safety was a 
key recommendation of both the royal comm ission and the Independent Taskforce on 
Workplace Health and Safety. It signals the st ep change required in the regulation of 
health and safety in the workplace.  
WorkSafe New Zealand will play a significant role in achieving this Government’s 
target of reducing workplace fatalities a nd serious injury rates by 25 percent by 2020. 
This goal should be representative of the type of approach that this new regulator should 
take. Improving health and safety is not ab out simply giving people checklists and 
telling them what to do; it is about letting them know what they need to achieve so that 
they can then set about achieving that.  
Part 2 of the bill amends the Health and Safety in Employment  Act to provide the 
necessary statutory support for the new mini ng regulations. This includes establishing 
new classes of duty-holder under the Act, specifically “mine worker” and “mine 
operator”. It also includes a definition of the mining operations that will be covered by 
the new regulatory regime for mining. This will include all surface and underground 
mines and some quarries and tunnels.  
Part 2 also provides for enhanced worker  participation arrangements in the mining 
industry. The provisions strengthen worker part icipation in health and safety in the 
mining industry and, in particular, the f unctions and powers of health and safety 
representatives. At the same time it ensures there are appropriate checks and balances to 
prevent undue interference in the day-to-day running of mining operations.  
All mining operations will be required to have a documented worker participation 
system, and this system will cover all mine workers at a site, including contractors and 
subcontractors and their employees. The functio ns and powers of site health and safety 
representatives will be explicit ly set out in the legislation. These include the ability for 
suitably trained representatives to perform in spections and stop operations if there is an 
imminent risk of serious harm occurring. Th e bill also establishes a new position of an 
industry-wide health and safety representati ve to provide, in the royal commission’s 
words, an extra set of eyes and ears and a further line of defence. 
 These positions can be appointed and f unded either by a union or by another group 
of mine workers. The functions and powers of  both site and industr y health and safety 
representatives will be balanced by provisions that ensure the health and safety 
representatives carry out thei r functions only for health a nd safety purposes, and do not 
unnecessarily impede production.  
Part 3 of the bill ensures that the legislation that supports the Mines Rescue service is 
fit for purpose today. The Mines Rescue se rvice plays a crucial role in emergency 
response. The royal commission recommended th at the Mines Rescue Trust Act better 
reflect the functions that the service actually carries out, and that there be a review of 
the adequacy and fairness of the levy that f unds the service. Part  3 also reflects the 
Government’s decision to broaden the respons e to the royal commission to other forms 
of mining as well as underground coalmining. It does so by expanding the coverage of 
27 Jun 2013 Health and Safety (Pik e River Implementation) Bill 11375 
the Mines Rescue service. The governance of the Mines Rescue Trus t is also amended 
to reflect this change in coverage.  
The Mines Rescue service has unique expert ise in training and equipping brigades to 
respond to emergencies, assisting mine ope rators in emergency preparedness and 
deploying brigades, and providi ng advice to mine operators during emergencies. All of 
these capabilities will be reflected in the new functions of the Mines Rescue service 
provided for in the bill.  
The bill also enables the levy that funds the service to be set in regulations. Officials 
are currently developing proposals to ensure that the levy adequate ly covers the core 
functions of the service while remaining fa ir and proportionate for the mine operators 
that will be required to pay it.  
The introduction and considera tion of this bill is happening in parallel with public 
consultation on the wider package of propos als for the new regulatory regime for 
mining. Although the consultation mainly con cerns the proposed mining regulations, it 
also covers the worker participation and mines rescue elements of this bill. This parallel 
process is necessary to meet the commitmen t to implement the response to the royal 
commission’s recommendations by the end of this year.  
Submitters have been advised that their submissions on these issues will be taken 
into account when officials advise the G overnment and the select committee on any 
changes that may be needed to the bill. The public discussion paper also informs likely 
submitters of this bill, and invites them to  get involved in the public submission process 
on it.  
This Government has made a commitment to the families of the victims of the Pike 
River mine to ensure that we follow through on every recommendation of the royal 
commission. If there can be any good from the tragic loss of lives, then let it be 
movement from platitudes to action, and a cr eation of frameworks that will shape better 
behaviour and outcomes in the workplace. This b ill is an important step in this process, 
and will improve workplace health and safety in the mining sector and beyond in New 
Zealand. I commend this bill to the House.

 Clause 7 then goes on to talk a bout business generally. The governance

making judgments on what was right and what  was not right for the safety of people

It is a lesson for officials. Officials work  under pressure and they do not always have

who were prepared to work for bonuses, w ho were prepared to forgo some of the 
lessons of the past in order to get the coal out of the ground. The lessons for the officials

For company directors there is a lesson here. You may flit around from one company

The people who went to that company, Pike River Coal, looking to get a good return for

at the coalface, ask the people in the comp any what is going on, and take responsibility

There is a lesson for the miners. Their enthus iasm to work with one another in risky 
environments, to get on and do the job, to gr ow the project, and to deliver incomes for 
their families, incomes for their mates, and income for the community is something we

In the 1980s and 1990s New Zealand experi enced a wave of change, underpinned by

It is worth taking the time to remind ourselv es what this bill is about. This bill is 
squarely about safety. It was prompted by concerns about untested substances being 
sold with no controls. The Government c ould have banned indivi dual substances once 
we found out what they were, but this process was reactive and extremely time-
consuming. For each banned substance th e Government had to identify what the 
substance was and identify possible harm fr om it before any action could be taken. 
Unfortunately the realities of living in th is technological age meant that there were 
always new ones waiting with the potentia l to cause more harm. The number of 
substances available, potentially thousands, meant this was ne ver going to be more than 
a temporary fix.  
This bill will fix this problem once and fo r all. No longer will the onus be on the 
Government to show a risk of harm; the onus will be on anyone wanting to produce a 
psychoactive product to show it  poses no more than a low risk of harm. In order to do 
that, there must be a way in which producer s can demonstrate that their product meets 
the standard. But even if pr oducts meet that standard, th e Government will still be 
insisting on tight controls around their availability. For starters, from day one of 
enactment, neighbourhood dairies will no longer be entitled to stock any such product, 
nor will sales to those under 18 years of ag e be permitted. These restrictions were 
always the Government’s intention, but I a ppreciate the Health Committee’s wish to 
have that detailed in the primary register—legislation rather than regulations.

to read it through and you can work out the big words that way.

occur, provide absolute certainty that the G overnment is serious about controlling these

Other changes made in the select comm ittee include some clarification of the 
principle and purpose of this bill. The ne w version of the bill clarifies that the

select committee also inserted a principle th at a product that meets a standard will be 
approved. If there really  are products that meet these te sts and pose only a low risk of 
harm, then they will be approved. This bill was never meant to be a ban by stealth; it is 
about providing safer communities for our young people in particular.

of an unapproved product and possession of  any psychoactive substance by people 
under 18. I know that a lot of submitters want ed no personal possession offence, and I 
respect that view. Submitters raised a concern, in particular, about young people having 
their future travel and employment opti ons blighted through yout hful foolishness. I 
agree that this would be an undesirable outcome. This bill is not about establishing a 
new class of criminal, but I do not think reco gnising that there still needs to be some 
personal responsibility taken is a bad thing. However, I can assure those who argued 
against a personal possession prov ision that we have very carefully made sure no one

to prevent.  
Another issue raised was the impact of these products on local communities. The

particular. In response, the bill now contai ns provisions allowing local authorities to 
restrict outlet locations  and density, similar to the provi sions in the Sale and Supply of

an issue that many, if not most, people feel very strongly about. Let me say now that I 
respect those feelings and I share them. If th ere are suitable non-anim al tests, then they 
must and will be used. This bill is a response to the harm  caused by untested products, 
and the countervailing consideration must be human safety. We must be sure that the 
tests that these products are put  through give us robust inform ation so that the regulator 
can make sound decisions. Whether or not there is a suitable non-animal test is a matter 
for the experts.  
The Ministry of Health established an interim expert committee, including experts on 
toxicology, pharmacology, and animal welfar e. Mr Dunne asked that committee for 
advice on non-animal tests, clearly articula ting his strong preference for a regime that 
excluded animal testing. The committee’s advice was that some animal testing would be 
necessary at first to ensure that the ri sk of products was accurately assessed. The 
committee went on to advise that there were some alternative tests that could be used 
immediately, and that it would continue to work to identify other alternatives.  
After receiving this advice I asked the Health Committee to consider an amendment

advisory committee to actively seek alterna tives. I am very plea sed to say that the 
committee members agreed unanimously to these amendments, which are in clause 11A 
of the revised bill. The expert advisory committee will actively seek alternatives to 
animal tests, and, again, I want to make it clear that there will be no animal testing 
where there is a suitable alternative. The ove rriding principle remains the need to make 
sure that the products sold in New Zealand pose no more than a low risk of harm. The 
importance of that principle is why this bill is before the House.

Policy. Although there will be separate discus sions and consultations held to discuss

Hon JOHN BANKS (Leader—ACT): I rise to oppose the Psychoactive Substances 
Bill, and I will oppose it at ever y turn until it ends up on the statute book with the 
numbers, except for me, in this House. This bill is well intentione d—there is no doubt

I find it totally unacceptable that this bill fails to rule out—to rule out—testing these 
recreational drugs on innocent animals. Protec ting animals is ingrained in my soul. I 
think most New Zealanders will be outraged at the idea that chemicals people use just 
for fun can be, and likely will be, tested on harmless animals. Animals will be put to 
extreme pain, animals will suffer, and animals will die. That is why the countries in the 
European Union have banned the testing of cosmetics on animals—in particular, 
rabbits.  
We must remember that psychoactive drug substances are not a necessity, and we 
should say to people today, from this Parlia ment, that they are high-risk substances 
under any circumstances—they are not a n ecessity for the well-being of the human 
person. Recreational drugs are not something one needs to consume. They are not 
something people should consume. We should say, from this Parliament today, that 
young people, any person, should not be consum ing these substances. That is the first 
message. They are not lifesaving medicines or  something that will relieve suffering. 
People do not need to take these chemicals.  
Their prolific use will cause widespread  animal suffering. There is simply no 
justification or reason for unnecessary drugs like these to be tested on animals, and I for 
one find it deeply offensive that any Gove rnment would sanction this. Animals will be 
in pain and animals will die in the name of people wanting to take mind-altering drugs 
on the weekend. That is simply wrong and una cceptable. Animals must not experience 
suffering for economic or entertainment reasons , or for lining the pockets of the drug 
importers and the drug dealers who will be selling them at the dairies to addle the minds 
of our kids.  
I know the Health Committee inserted a new cl ause in the bill to state that animal 
testing should be used only when necessary. But animal testing will  never be necessary 
for recreational drug purposes. It will never be  necessary to cruelly treat a beagle puppy 
in the name of a recreational party drug. Evidence shows animal testing is not necessary 
at all to prove the safety of these mind- altering chemicals. Dr Ian Shaw of the 
University of Canterbury says that non-animal  testing can adequately establish whether 
11402 Psychoactive Substances Bill 27 Jun 2013 
a substance has an unacceptable risk of acute toxicity. Cell culture, ex vivo, and 
structure-activity relationship studies can all be used to establish the risk. Non-animal 
testing regimes can test all of these substances to establish the risk.  
I cannot for the life of me see the misc hief in allowing the good people of Save 
Animals from Exploitation and the SPCA to come to the select committee to make a 
submission. What would have been the mischi ef of saying to these good Samaritans in 
our community who protect harmless animals from cruelty: “Come to the select 
committee of the Parliament and have your say.”? I know why they were not allowed. It 
was because the ex - Associate Minister of  Health would have been embarrassed by 
what they would have had to say about our ob ligations to treat animals with respect and 
dignity.  
This afternoon in the House the ex - Associ ate Minister said: “It’s not our intention 
to test these substances on animals.” He said  it four times: “It’s not our intention.” I 
interjected from that seat there: “Tell me, ex-Minister, will animals be used for 
testing?”. He said: “It’s not our intenti on.” The road to hell is paved with good 
intentions. I asked the ex-Minister four times. The naive ex-Minister said “It’s not our 
intention. It’s never been our intention.”, but that is not what the bill says. The bill does 
not rule out the testing on beagle puppies of these mind-altering, dangerous chemicals. 
It does not rule it out.  
There would be no mischief whatsoever in taking Mojo Mathers’ Supplementary 
Order Paper 260 and embracing it, and then we would have worl d-class, leading 
legislation on mind-altering s ubstances that will be sold  by the drug dealers and the 
dairies on the corner, mainly to our young pe ople. We would have that there. What 
would have been the mischief ? What would have been th e mischief of taking Mojo 
Mathers’ Supplementary Order Paper? It wa s a pigheaded attitude by the ex-Minister 
that stopped it, and nothing more. I know my friends in the National Party on the select 
committee would not have worried if that had been the directive from the ex-Minister. 
But the ex-Minister could not see it in his heart and in his soul to protect harmless 
animals from being treated with these dangerous drugs.  
If you cannot prove your fun dr ug of choice is safe without  putting animals in abject 
misery, you cannot sell the drug. If you need to pay more for more expensive, non-
animal testing in China, where it will be tested, I say tough luck, again. That is the price 
you pay, and that is the price you have to pay for the profiteers of these dangerous 
chemicals who sell them to our kids. The real ity is the bill could well result in drugs 
being tested on animals in places like China and India, where animal welfare is 
shamefully non-existent. Most of these substanc es will be tested in China and in India, 
where there are no animal welfare rights, no animal welfare care, and no responsibility.  
The statement in the bill that overseas test ing must be carried out in accordance with 
the New Zealand Animal Welfare Act is nonsen se because there is no way for us in 
New Zealand to assess what goes on in the torture chambers of animal testing 
laboratories in South-east Asia . There is no way we can test  there. There is no way we

world-leading education. I repeat these words: as the most powerful creatures on this

BARBARA STEWART (NZ First) : I stand on behalf of New Zealand First to

was a very constructive process, helped out by the committee officials.  
Ideally—and before we went to the se lect committee—New Zealand First would

during the select committee process we ha d our opinions changed, because these 
products contain many ingredients that ar e commonly available for purchase now. Of

continually monitor these dr ugs, and placing every dodgy s ubstance on the misuse of 
drugs register when it became a problem. Consequently, the Government was always 
left two steps behind, running to try to catch  up, and that is not a good situation when 
the Government is actually supposed to be running the country.  
New Zealand First supports this bill because it actually protects the health and safety 
of New Zealanders, which is most importa nt. We know that legal highs are largely 
detrimental to our nation’s health. Unfortunately, they are lucrative to the manufacturers

data to support human research in order to allow the legislation to deliver its primary 
aim. The Committee recommends that some anim al testing be permitted.” I think that is 
very, very important to underscore. 
The final point is this: having looked very ca refully at the intern ational best-practice 
scientific community, there is  no question but that animal  testing—though it should be 
minimised—is necessary. Undoubtedly, rigorous  testing is required to demonstrate 
minimal risk, particularly when tens of thousands of users are young adults and 
adolescents. I very much hope that the La bour Party—given that it s current leader, Mr 
Shearer, is also its scien ce spokesman—will support an evidence-based approach and 
support his health team. Not to do so, I believe, would be utterly irresponsible. 
Just to end, there is no question but that the major purpose of this bill is excellent. It 
is to regulate psychoactive substances and to  protect the health of, and minimise harm 
to, individuals who use them in this country. Thank you. 
CLARE CURRAN (Labour—Dunedin South) : I welcome the opportunity to 
speak at the second reading of this bill, th e Psychoactive Substances Bill. It is an 
important opportunity to talk about the absolute hope that is  out there in the 
communities throughout New Zealand that this  bill is going through the House as 
quickly as possible, and that it will go some way to addressing some of the terrible harm 
that is being done in our community by the ps ychoactive substances that are prevalent. 
First of all, I would like to just put on th e record—if it has not b een put on the record 
27 Jun 2013 Psychoactive Substances Bill 11407 
already—my congratulations to our spokesper son on this bill, Iain Lees-Galloway, who 
has done such a great job on pushing this forw ard. It was he who sa id very loudly last 
year that this change should be happening and should have happened sooner. In fact, he 
said that we think it is ridiculous that we have basically been experimenting on our kids 
by allowing the substances to come on the shelf, and then constantly chasing our tails 
trying to get them off the shel f again. That absolutely encapsulates just what has been 
happening in communities throughout New Zealand. Although I certainly do also 
acknowledge my colleague Louisa Wall, who has been working extremely hard in her 
community in Manurewa, there are many othe r communities for which this is a terrible 
scourge and in which there are terrible harms being done.  
I want to talk in my speech on this bill about some of the harm that has been done in 
my community in Dunedin, but before I do that I would also like to just point out that it 
must be said that this Government has not taken the opportunity to completely overhaul 
the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. In 1975 many of  the people who are standing in this 
House were not even born. Many things have actually moved on since then. 
Hon Trevor Mallard: Ha, ha! 
CLARE CURRAN : Not all of the members of th e House—some of them were 
probably sitting in this House in 1975, but onl y a very few. But certainly times have 
changed, and, as we know, the composition of drugs has changed, the way that they are 
being taken has changed, and our ability to re spond to drug abuse has changed. The 
only thing that has not changed is the law.  
I just want to say what ha s actually brought me to be sp eaking about this particular 
issue today. It was th e community that came into my of fice earlier this year and raised 
this with me. There was a stream of pe ople from the community talking about the 
absolute importance of making change ha ppen and making change quickly, and the 
impact that this problem has had on so  many young people in the community. For 
example, there was the woman who came into  my office to offer me her support and 
give me her story on how she had been affected by taking these drugs. She had just 
come out of a psychiatric institution.
